blocks.text:
Almost every real Java program is concurrent. A web server handles thousands of requests at once; a desktop app keeps its window responsive while it downloads a file; a batch job splits a large input across all CPU cores. Concurrency is also the area of Java where the most subtle bugs live: bugs that appear once a week in production, vanish under a debugger, and corrupt data silently. This chapter builds the vocabulary and the mental model you need before you write your first thread. The rest of this Part builds on it.

### Processes and threads

A **process** is a running program. The operating system gives each process its own private virtual address space, its own open files and its own resources. Two processes cannot read each other's memory unless they use an explicit mechanism (pipes, sockets, shared memory). A Java program started with `java Main` is one process containing one JVM.

A **thread** is a path of execution inside a process. All threads of a process share the same memory (in Java: the same heap), but each thread has its own program counter and its own call stack holding its local variables. Every Java program has at least one thread, called `main`, plus several JVM-internal threads (garbage collector workers, JIT compiler threads, the signal dispatcher).

A crash is contained to the process
An uncaught error can corrupt state shared by all threads
blocks.caption: Process versus thread.

blocks.text:
The sharing is what makes threads both powerful and dangerous. Communication between threads is nearly free (you just read a field), but nothing stops two threads from changing the same field at the same moment.

### Concurrency versus parallelism

These two words are often used as if they meant the same thing. They do not.

- **Concurrency** is about *structure*: dealing with many things at once. Several tasks are in progress and their execution overlaps in time. A single CPU core can run a concurrent program by switching rapidly between tasks (time slicing).
- **Parallelism** is about *execution*: doing many things at the same instant. It needs more than one CPU core.

A concurrent program may run in parallel when cores are available, but it is still correct on one core. A good mental picture: one cook switching between three pans is concurrent; three cooks each with a pan is parallel.

There are two quite different reasons to use threads:

1. **To hide waiting (I/O-bound work).** A thread that waits for a database or a network reply does not need a CPU. While it waits, other threads can run. Here threads improve throughput and responsiveness even on one core.
2. **To use more cores (CPU-bound work).** Splitting a computation across cores shortens the wall-clock time, up to the limits described next.

Choosing the wrong model is a classic mistake. Adding 200 threads to a CPU-bound task on 4 cores does not make it 50 times faster; it adds scheduling overhead. Adding threads to an I/O-bound task, on the other hand, can multiply throughput until the remote system becomes the bottleneck.

### Why concurrent programming is hard

Sequential code has one property you rely on without noticing: statement N finishes before statement N+1 starts, and each statement sees the effects of all earlier ones. With threads, three things break that comfort.

#### Atomicity

An operation is **atomic** if no other thread can observe it half-done. `count++` looks like one operation but is three: read the field, add one, write it back. Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, so one increment is lost. You will reproduce this in the next chapters.

#### Visibility

When one thread writes a variable, there is no guarantee, by default, that another thread will ever see the new value. Each CPU core has caches and registers, and the compiler and the JIT are free to keep a value in a register for the whole length of a loop. Visibility is the property that a write by one thread becomes observable by another.

#### Ordering

The JIT compiler and the CPU may reorder independent instructions to run faster. Within one thread the result is always as if the code ran in order, but a second thread watching the writes can see them in a different order from the one you wrote. The Java Memory Model (next chapters) defines exactly when you can rely on an order.

These three (atomicity, visibility, ordering) are the entire reason for every tool in this Part: `synchronized`, `volatile`, atomics, locks and concurrent collections each guarantee some combination of them.

### CPU caches in one picture

Why can a value be invisible? Because a modern CPU does not read main memory on every access. It reads through small, very fast caches.

**Simplified view of a two-core machine**

blocks.code:
Core 0                      Core 1
+-----------+              +-----------+
| registers |              | registers |
| L1 cache  |              | L1 cache  |     per core: fast, tiny (tens of KB)
| L2 cache  |              | L2 cache  |     per core or per core pair
+-----+-----+              +-----+-----+
      |                          |
      +------------+-------------+
                   |
             L3 cache (shared)
                   |
              main memory (RAM)               shared: big, slow

blocks.text:
Hardware keeps caches *coherent* (a write on one core eventually invalidates stale copies on others), but "eventually" and "in which order" are exactly what the hardware is allowed to be loose about, in exchange for speed. Typical latencies, as orders of magnitude: a register access is under a nanosecond, L1 about a nanosecond, L3 tens of nanoseconds, main memory around a hundred nanoseconds. A thread that reads a variable repeatedly will happily keep using its cached or register copy.

The practical consequence: Java does not promise that threads share a single consistent "current value" of every variable. It promises something weaker and precisely specified, the Java Memory Model, that you opt into with `synchronized`, `volatile`, `final` and the `java.util.concurrent` classes.

### How much faster can parallelism make things? (Amdahl's law)

Suppose a fraction `p` of a job can be parallelised and the rest, `1 - p`, must run sequentially. With `n` cores the best possible speed-up is

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: Amdahl's law speedup(n) = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n) Even with unlimited cores the speed-up is capped at 1 / (1 - p). A job that is 90 percent parallel can never go more than 10 times faster.

blocks.title: Amdahl.java

blocks.code:
$ java Amdahl.java
cores available here: 2 (varies)
parallel fraction 0.50:  n=2 -> 1.33x  n=4 -> 1.60x  n=8 -> 1.78x  n=16 -> 1.88x  n=1000 -> 2.00x
parallel fraction 0.90:  n=2 -> 1.82x  n=4 -> 3.08x  n=8 -> 4.71x  n=16 -> 6.40x  n=1000 -> 9.91x
parallel fraction 0.95:  n=2 -> 1.90x  n=4 -> 3.48x  n=8 -> 5.93x  n=16 -> 9.14x  n=1000 -> 19.63x
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice: going from 16 to 1000 cores buys a 90-percent-parallel job only 6.4x to 9.9x. The sequential part, often a lock that all threads must pass through, dominates. This is why reducing the time spent holding locks (a theme of the synchronization chapters) matters more than adding hardware. Amdahl's law is optimistic: it ignores the cost of coordination, which grows with the number of threads.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism? Concurrency is about managing several tasks whose execution overlaps in time, which a single core can do by time slicing. Parallelism is executing several tasks at the same instant on multiple cores. Concurrency is a property of the program's structure; parallelism is a property of its execution. You can have concurrency without parallelism (one core), and the reason you design for concurrency is partly to be able to exploit parallel hardware.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In a Spring Boot service every incoming HTTP request is handled on a thread taken from a pool. Your singleton beans, such as services and repositories, are therefore shared by many threads at once. That is why "keep singleton beans stateless" is the first rule of Spring code: a mutable field in a service is a data race waiting to happen.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Concurrency is the structure of overlapping tasks; parallelism is simultaneous execution on several cores.

- Threads share the heap, which makes communication cheap and bugs easy.
- The three hazards are atomicity, visibility and ordering; every concurrency tool in Java addresses some of them.
- CPU caches and the optimiser mean threads do not automatically see each other's writes.
- Amdahl's law: the sequential fraction caps the speed-up, so shorten critical sections.
- Use threads to hide I/O waits or to spread CPU work over about as many threads as cores.

A **thread** in Java is an object of class `java.lang.Thread` that represents an operating-system thread (a *platform* *thread*; Java 21 adds cheap *virtual threads*, covered in a later chapter). This chapter shows how to create threads, how their life cycle works, how to wait for them, and, most importantly, how to stop them politely.

### Creating and starting threads

You tell a thread *what to run* by giving it a `Runnable` (a functional interface with one method, `void run()`), either by passing it to the `Thread` constructor or by subclassing `Thread` and overriding `run`. Passing a `Runnable` is almost always better: it separates the task from the mechanism that runs it, so the same task can later be handed to an executor.

blocks.title: Basics.java

blocks.code:
$ java Basics.java
lambda in Thread-0
Task in worker-A
subclass in worker-B
Task in main
main is main, id>0: true
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `start()` asks the JVM to create the OS thread and call `run()` on it. The thread that called `start()` continues immediately.
- Calling `run()` directly (the `never-started` line) executes the method on the *calling* thread. The output says `Task in` `main`. This is one of the most common beginner bugs: no concurrency happens at all.
- A thread can be started only once. A second `start()` throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.
- Unnamed threads get names `Thread-0`, `Thread-1`, and so on. Always name threads you create (constructor argument or `setName`); names show up in thread dumps and logs, which is where you will need them. `Thread.threadId()` (Java 19+) replaces the deprecated `getId()`.

In Java 21 there are also builders: `Thread.ofPlatform().name("worker-", 0).start(task)` and `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)`. In application code you will usually not create threads by hand at all but submit tasks to an `ExecutorService`, which is the topic of a later chapter. Understanding raw threads is still essential, because executors are built from them.

### The thread life cycle

blocks.text: The following program drives one thread through every state and prints what `getState()` reports. The `sleep` calls here are only to give the thread time to reach the next state; real code must never coordinate threads with sleeps.

blocks.title: States.java

blocks.code:
$ java States.java
before start : NEW
lock held    : BLOCKED
sleeping     : TIMED_WAITING
in wait()    : WAITING
after finish : TERMINATED
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Main holds `lock` while it starts `demo`, so `demo` is BLOCKED at its first `synchronized`. After main releases the lock, `demo` sleeps (TIMED\_WAITING), then calls `lock.wait()` (WAITING) until main calls `notify()`. A thread in `BLOCKED` is waiting for a *lock*; in `WAITING` it is waiting for a *signal*. Telling these apart in a thread dump is the first step in diagnosing a hung application.

### Waiting for a thread: join

`t.join()` blocks the calling thread until `t` terminates, and it also creates a happens-before edge (everything `t` wrote is visible to the caller afterwards; see the memory model chapter). `join(millis)` gives up after a timeout; check `isAlive()` afterwards to see whether the thread really finished. Always prefer `join` (or a `Future`, later) over sleeping and hoping.

### Daemon threads and JVM exit

The JVM exits when all *non-daemon* threads have finished. A **daemon thread** is a background helper (a cache cleaner, a heartbeat) that must not keep the JVM alive. Call `setDaemon(true)` *before* `start()`. A thread inherits the daemon status of the thread that creates it. Daemon threads are stopped abruptly at exit: `finally` blocks and `try`-with-resources cleanup do not run, so never use a daemon for work that must complete or for anything holding files or locks that need orderly release.

### Uncaught exceptions

If `run()` throws, the exception does not propagate to the thread that called `start()`; there is no one to catch it. By default the JVM prints the stack trace to `System.err` and the thread dies. You can install a handler per thread (`setUncaughtExceptionHandler`) or globally (`Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler`) to log and alert. In thread pools the story differs (exceptions are captured into the `Future`), which a later chapter shows.

blocks.title: Daemon.java

blocks.code:
$ java Daemon.java
handler got java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom from bad-thread
main ends; daemon=true
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
The daemon thread would sleep 5 seconds and print, but `main` ends first, no non-daemon thread remains, and the JVM exits at once; the message never appears.

### Interruption: the cooperative cancellation protocol

How do you stop a thread? Not with `Thread.stop()`: it was deprecated for removal because it kills a thread at an arbitrary point, leaving objects half-updated and locks released in an inconsistent state; in Java 20 it was changed to throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. Java's mechanism is **interruption**, which is a polite request. Interrupting a thread sets its *interrupt flag*; it is up to the thread's code to notice and stop.

The rules form a small protocol:

1. `t.interrupt()` sets the flag on `t`.
2. A thread in a blocking method that supports it (`sleep`, `wait`, `join`, `BlockingQueue.put/take`, most `java.util.concurrent` waits) wakes up, **clears the flag**, and throws `InterruptedException`.
3. A busy loop must poll `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` itself.
4. `Thread.interrupted()` (static) returns the flag *and clears it*; avoid it unless you mean to consume the interrupt.

blocks.title: Interrupt.java

blocks.code:
$ java Interrupt.java
sleeper: caught, flag now false
sleeper: restored, flag now true
spinner: saw interrupt, stopping
done
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: What to notice: when `InterruptedException` is thrown the flag is already cleared (`flag now false`). If you swallow the exception the request to stop is lost forever. The correct handling is one of two things: **propagate** the exception (declare `throws InterruptedException`), or **restore the flag** with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` so callers up the stack can still see it.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never write `catch (InterruptedException e) { }` (an empty catch) or just print and continue. The thread was asked to stop and you ignored it. Executors that try to shut down will hang, and tasks that should be cancelled will keep running. Either rethrow, or call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` and return.

### Priorities, yield and other myths

`setPriority(1..10)` is only a hint to the OS scheduler. On Linux, JVM thread priorities are ignored by default, and on other systems they have platform-specific effects. Never use priorities for correctness (for example to make "the important thread always win"). `Thread.yield()` is likewise a hint, and `Thread.sleep(0)` is not a reliable way to let others run. If one thread must run before another, use synchronisation (`join`, latches, locks), never timing or priorities.

`Thread.sleep(ms)` pauses the current thread without releasing any monitor it holds. This makes sleeping inside a `synchronized` block a good way to stall every other thread that needs that lock. (`Object.wait()`, by contrast, releases the monitor.)

### Naming and reading a thread dump

A **thread dump** is a snapshot of all threads, their states and stacks. You get it with `jstack <pid>` or `jcmd <pid>` `Thread.print`, or by sending the process a `SIGQUIT` with `kill -3 <pid>` (Linux/macOS), which prints the dump to the program's standard output. Every thread appears with its name, daemon flag, `prio`, native id and `java.lang.Thread.State`. A later chapter reads one in anger when diagnosing a deadlock. For now: if your threads are all called `Thread-17`, you cannot tell the order-processing thread from the e-mail thread. Name them.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Create threads with a descriptive name and, in library code, a stable prefix (for example `inventory-sync-1`). When something hangs at 3 a.m. the name is the first clue.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between `start()` and `run()`? `start()` creates a new OS thread and makes the JVM call `run()` on it; control returns immediately to the caller. Calling `run()` directly is just an ordinary method call on the current thread, so there is no concurrency. `start()` can be called only once per `Thread` object.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you stop a thread safely? Use cooperative interruption: call `interrupt()`, and make the target thread check `isInterrupted()` in loops and handle `InterruptedException` by cleaning up and exiting (or restoring the interrupt flag). `Thread.stop()` is unsafe and no longer works. A `volatile boolean` flag also works for loops that never block, but interruption additionally wakes blocked threads.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Thread basics to remember.

- Create threads from a `Runnable`; call `start()`, never `run()`; name your threads.
- Six states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED (lock), WAITING and TIMED\_WAITING (signal or time), TERMINATED.
- `join()` waits for termination and gives visibility of the thread's writes.
- Stop threads with interruption: handle `InterruptedException` by propagating it or restoring the flag; never swallow it.
- Priorities and `yield` are hints; never rely on them. The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain.

sections.title: Races and the Java Memory Model

blocks.text:
Two threads, one counter, no locks. What could go wrong? This chapter shows, by running code, three different ways it goes wrong, and then introduces the rulebook that tells you exactly when a multi-threaded Java program is guaranteed to behave: the **Java Memory Model** (JMM), defined in chapter 17 of the Java Language Specification.

### A race condition you can run

A **race condition** exists when the correctness of a computation depends on the relative timing of threads. The simplest case is a lost update. The program below increments four counters from two threads, one million times each. One counter is a plain `int`, one is `volatile`, one is guarded by `synchronized`, and one is an `AtomicInteger`.

blocks.title: Race.java

blocks.text: Compile it and run it a few times (we use `javac` here because the single-file launcher shows slightly different timing):

blocks.code:
$ javac Race.java && java Race
expected          : 2000000
plain int         : 1999592
volatile int      : 1895976
synchronized      : 2000000
AtomicInteger     : 2000000
$ java Race
expected          : 2000000
plain int         : 1999886
volatile int      : 1999889
synchronized      : 2000000
AtomicInteger     : 2000000
blocks.title: Typical output (varies between runs)

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- The plain `int` loses updates. How many it loses changes from run to run (this build machine has only 2 cores, so the loss is small; on a busier or bigger machine it is much larger). A bug whose symptom changes every run is typical of a race.
- `volatile` **does not fix it.** `vol++` is still read, add, write. Volatility makes each individual read and write visible, but the three steps can interleave. (This is the most common misconception about `volatile`.)
- `synchronized` and `AtomicInteger` give exactly 2000000, for different reasons that later chapters explain: mutual exclusion and a hardware compare-and-swap loop.
- Races may not show if you test once. A program that passes a hundred test runs can still be wrong. You prove thread safety by reasoning with the rules below, not by testing.

#### What count++ really is

**Three steps in bytecode, interleaved by two threads**

blocks.code:
Thread A: getstatic count   -> 5
Thread B: getstatic count   -> 5
Thread A: iconst_1, iadd    -> 6
Thread B: iconst_1, iadd    -> 6
Thread A: putstatic count   <- 6
Thread B: putstatic count   <- 6      one increment is lost; count is 6, not 7

blocks.text:
This is a **check-then-act** / **read-modify-write** problem. The cure is to make the whole compound action atomic.

### Visibility: the flag that never flips

The second hazard needs no interleaving at all. One thread writes a flag; another loops until it sees it.

blocks.title: Visibility.java

blocks.code:
$ javac Visibility.java && java Visibility
main set stop = true
worker alive after 2s: true
blocks.title: Compile with javac and run (typical; HotSpot with default JIT)

blocks.text: The worker never stops. The JIT compiler may legally hoist the read of `stop` out of the loop (it sees no code in the loop that changes it, so it assumes it can read it once). Make the field `volatile` and the program behaves:

blocks.title: VisibilityFixed.java

blocks.code:
$ javac VisibilityFixed.java && java VisibilityFixed
main set stop = true
worker saw stop flag; spins=true
worker alive after 2s: false
blocks.title: Run it
Gotcha
blocks.text: This bug is not guaranteed to appear. Under the source launcher (`java Visibility.java`) on the build machine the loop happened to terminate, while the javac-compiled class hung. Whether the JIT optimises the loop depends on timing, flags and JVM version. Without `volatile` the program is *incorrect* even on the days it works.

### Reordering

The third hazard is order. Consider two threads where `x`, `y`, `r1`, `r2` start at 0:

**Classic reordering litmus test**

blocks.code: Thread A:  x = 1;  r1 = y;        Thread B:  y = 1;  r2 = x;

blocks.text:
Intuition says at least one thread must see the other's write, so `r1 == 0 && r2 == 0` is impossible. On real hardware it *is* possible, because each core buffers its write in a store buffer and may execute the following read before the write becomes visible to others (and the JIT may also swap the two statements, since they touch different variables). Seeing the effect in a Java test needs millions of precise attempts on a multi-core machine, and our 2-core build machine did not show it reliably, so we do not print a number here; tools such as the JCStress harness exist for exactly this. The lesson is that you may not infer anything about cross-thread order from the order of statements in the source.

### The Java Memory Model in plain words

The JMM does not describe caches and store buffers. It defines a relation between actions called **happens-before** (written hb). If action A happens-before action B, then A's effects (all its writes) are visible to B, and A is ordered before B. If there is no happens-before edge between a write and a read of the same variable, that is a **data race**, and the read may return the latest write, an older write, or a value written by some interleaving; the specification only promises each read sees *some* write, not which one.

blocks.text: The main happens-before rules (what you may rely on):

rows: Each action in a thread happens-before every later action in the same thread.
An `unlock` of a monitor happens-before every later `lock` of that same monitor.
A write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of that field.
Every action in `t` happens-before another thread detects that `t` ended (`t.join()` returns, or `t.isAlive()` is false).
Writes in a constructor to `final` fields happen-before any thread reads them through a reference obtained after the constructor ends (the freeze rule).
If A hb B and B hb C then A hb C.
blocks.caption: Happens-before rules.

blocks.text:
Transitivity is the magic that makes this usable. Thread A writes ordinary data, then writes a volatile flag. Thread B reads the volatile flag (true), then reads the ordinary data. Because the data write hb the flag write (program order), flag write hb flag read (volatile rule), and flag read hb data read (program order), B is guaranteed to see the data. This is called *piggybacking* on the volatile.

Many library classes establish hb edges for you: submitting a task to an `ExecutorService` happens-before the task runs, the task's completion happens-before `Future.get()` returns, putting an object in a `BlockingQueue` happens-before taking it, `CountDownLatch.countDown()` happens-before a successful `await()`.

### volatile in detail

A `volatile` field gives you:

1. **Visibility:** a read always sees the most recent write to that variable by any thread.
2. **Ordering:** no instruction before a volatile write is moved after it, and none after a volatile read is moved before it. It acts like a one-way fence at each access.
3. **Atomic reads and writes of** `long` **and** `double`**.** (The JLS allows a non-volatile 64-bit read or write to be split into two 32-bit halves; in practice 64-bit HotSpot does not tear them, but only `volatile` guarantees it.)

It does **not** give you atomic compound operations (`++`, check-then-act). Rules for using it: a single writer or writes that do not depend on the previous value (a status flag, a published reference, a configuration snapshot) are good fits.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What does `volatile` guarantee, and what does it not? It guarantees visibility (a read sees the last write) and ordering (via the happens-before edge from a write to later reads), and makes reads and writes of long and double atomic. It does not make compound actions such as `count++` atomic, because those are separate read and write steps; use `synchronized` or an atomic class for that.

### final fields and safe publication

Publishing an object means making a reference to it reachable by another thread. **Unsafe publication** is storing the reference in a plain shared field with no hb edge:

blocks.title: Fragment: unsafe publication

blocks.text:
A reader thread that sees `Holder.current != null` may still see `port == 0` or `env == null`: the reference write can become visible before the field writes inside the constructor. The object is *observed partially constructed*.

There are four standard ways to publish safely:

- Initialise the reference from a **static initialiser** (the class-initialisation lock gives an hb edge).
- Store it in a `volatile` **field** or an `AtomicReference`.
- Store it in a field guarded by a **lock** (readers lock the same monitor).
- Make the fields `final`. The freeze rule guarantees that any thread that sees the reference also sees the correctly constructed values of the final fields (and objects reachable only through them), even if the reference itself was published by a race. This is why immutable objects built from final fields are inherently thread-safe, as the last chapter of this Part discusses. The rule holds only if `this` does not escape from the constructor (do not start a thread or register a listener inside a constructor).

Also safe: placing the object in a thread-safe collection (`ConcurrentHashMap`, `BlockingQueue`) or handing it over through an executor.

### Double-checked locking

Lazy initialisation of a shared object is a famous trap. The "obvious" optimisation avoids locking after initialisation: check, lock, check again, create. Before Java 5 this was broken. It is correct today if and only if the field is `volatile`.

blocks.title: Singleton.java

blocks.code:
$ java Singleton.java
true
true
3
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice: without `volatile`, another thread could see `instance != null` yet see the `data` array not yet initialised, since the reference store may be reordered before the constructor's writes. The local variable `local` is a micro-optimisation (one volatile read on the fast path instead of two). The `Holder` class shows the simplest correct alternative: the **initialisation-on-demand holder idiom**. The JVM initialises `Holder.INSTANCE` lazily, the first time `Holder` is used, under the class-initialisation lock, so no explicit synchronisation is needed. For singletons, an `enum` with one constant is a third option. Prefer these over double-checked locking.

### Beyond volatile: VarHandle and fences

Since Java 9, `java.lang.invoke.VarHandle` offers finer-grained access modes to a field or array element: plain, opaque, acquire/release, and volatile, plus `compareAndSet`. The JDK's own atomic classes and concurrent collections are built on it (earlier on `sun.misc.Unsafe`). Application code should use `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicReference`, locks and the concurrent collections; reach for `VarHandle` only when you are writing a library data structure and have measured a need. Acquire/release semantics are weaker than full volatile but cheaper on some CPUs, and much easier to get wrong.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Safe code needs only two habits. First, every shared mutable variable must have a clear owner: guarded by one lock, declared volatile, or confined to one thread. Second, communicate between threads using library constructs that already carry the happens-before edges.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: A Spring `@Configuration` bean with `private final` fields is safely published to all request threads; a hand-rolled `static Map` cache written by one request thread and read by others is not. Frameworks initialise singletons under internal locks, which gives you an hb edge for the container's own beans, but not for state you mutate afterwards.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The memory model in short.

- `count++` is three steps; without mutual exclusion or an atomic, updates are lost, and tests will not reliably show it.
- Without a happens-before edge, a thread may never see another thread's write; the JIT may legally hoist a read out of a loop.
- Rules to learn: program order, monitor lock, volatile, thread start and join, final-field freeze, transitivity.
- `volatile` gives visibility and ordering, not atomic compound actions. Use it for flags and safely published references.
- Publish objects safely: static initialisers, volatile, locks or final fields. Prefer the holder idiom over double-checked locking.

The previous chapter showed that shared mutable state needs two things: **mutual exclusion** (only one thread at a time in a critical section) and **visibility** (what one thread wrote, the next sees). Java's built-in tool for both is the `synchronized` keyword, backed by an **intrinsic lock**, also called a **monitor**, that every Java object carries.

Every object has an associated monitor. Entering a `synchronized` block means acquiring that object's monitor; leaving it (normally *or by exception*) releases it. If another thread owns it, the entering thread becomes BLOCKED until the owner releases it. The compiler turns a block into `monitorenter` and `monitorexit` bytecodes (with an exception handler that guarantees the exit); a `synchronized` method is marked with the `ACC_SYNCHRONIZED` flag and the JVM acquires the lock on entry.

Because unlock happens-before the next lock of the same monitor, `synchronized` gives you visibility as well as exclusion: everything done inside the block is visible to the next thread that locks the same object.

#### Which object is the lock?
The two counters in the next listing use different locks: the instance counter locks the `Counter` object, the static one locks `Counter.class`. Both give the exact total.

blocks.title: Counter.java

blocks.code:
$ java Counter.java
2000000 2000000
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
The rule that matters: **two critical sections exclude each other only if they use the same lock object.** A static `synchronized` method and an instance `synchronized` method do not exclude each other, because they lock different objects. Likewise, if one thread updates a field under lock A and another reads it under lock B (or with no lock), there is no happens-before edge and you have a data race.

### Reentrancy

Intrinsic locks are **reentrant**: a thread that already owns a monitor can enter another block guarded by the same monitor, and it succeeds immediately. The JVM keeps a hold count and releases the monitor only when the count returns to zero. Without reentrancy a `synchronized` method could not call another `synchronized` method of the same object (or a subclass's overriding method) without deadlocking itself.

blocks.title: Reentrant.java

blocks.code:
$ java Reentrant.java
outer
inner, holds lock: true
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
### Method versus block, and lock scope

A `synchronized` method locks the whole method. A `synchronized` block locks only a few lines and lets you choose the lock object. Two guidelines:

1. **Keep critical sections short.** By Amdahl's law, time spent holding a lock is the sequential part of your program. Do not perform I/O, call unknown code or `sleep` while holding a lock; compute outside, then lock just to update shared state.
2. **Lock on a private object**, not on `this` or a public object, when you want to control who can participate:

blocks.title: Fragment: a private lock

blocks.text: If you synchronise on `this`, any code holding a reference to your object can take the same lock (`synchronized` `(inventory) { ... }`) and stall or deadlock you. Never lock on a `String` literal, a boxed `Integer`, or any value that might be shared or interned: unrelated code in the same JVM may be locking the same cached object. Never lock on a field you reassign, because threads would then lock different objects.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `synchronized` on only the setter, or only on writes, is not thread-safe. Every access (read and write) to the shared state must use the same lock, otherwise readers may see stale or inconsistent values.

### wait, notify and notifyAll

Mutual exclusion is not enough when a thread must wait for a *condition* ("the buffer has room", "the queue is not empty"). Spinning on the condition wastes CPU. The monitor provides three methods on `Object`:

- `wait()`: the calling thread must own the monitor; it **releases the monitor**, joins the object's wait set (WAITING) and sleeps until notified (or interrupted, or the timeout of `wait(ms)` passes). When it wakes, it must **re-acquire the** **monitor** before continuing.
- `notify()`: wakes one thread from the wait set (an arbitrary one).
- `notifyAll()`: wakes all threads in the wait set; they then compete for the monitor.

Calling any of them without owning the monitor throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`.

#### The rules of the wait loop

1. Always call `wait` **inside a loop that re-tests the condition**: `while (!condition) wait();`. Never `if`.
2. Always change the condition and notify while holding the same lock.
3. Prefer `notifyAll()` unless you can prove only one waiter kind exists and one wake-up suffices.

The loop is needed for three reasons. A thread woken by `notifyAll` may find that another thread already consumed the thing it wanted. The condition may be different for different waiters on the same monitor (producers and consumers). And the JVM is allowed to wake a waiting thread **spuriously**, without any notify, a behaviour inherited from OS threading libraries and documented in the Javadoc of `Object.wait`.

### Producer-consumer by hand

A bounded buffer is the standard example: producers wait when it is full, consumers wait when it is empty.

blocks.title: BoundedBuffer.java

blocks.code:
$ java BoundedBuffer.java
consumer sum = 36
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
The producer puts 1..8 (sum 36) and a poison pill. With capacity 3 the producer must repeatedly wait for room, and the consumer must wait for items, so the example exercises both waits. What to notice:

- Both methods are `synchronized`, so the queue (an unsynchronised `ArrayDeque`) is only touched under the monitor, and both conditions are tested in `while` loops.
- `notifyAll()` is used because producers and consumers wait for *different* conditions on the same monitor. A plain `notify()` could wake a producer when only a consumer can make progress, and then the wake-up is "lost": all threads sleep forever.
- `put` and `take` declare `InterruptedException` and propagate it, honouring the interruption protocol.

In real code you would use a `BlockingQueue` (a later chapter) which does all of this; but you must understand `wait`/`notify` because it is the foundation of those classes and a favourite interview topic.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why must `wait()` be called in a loop? Because a thread can wake without the condition being true: another thread may have consumed it first (a "stolen" wake-up), several conditions may share one monitor, and spurious wake-ups are permitted by the specification. The loop re-checks the condition after each wake-up and waits again if it is still false.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between `sleep()` and `wait()`? `sleep` is a static `Thread` method; it pauses the current thread and does NOT release any lock. `wait` is an `Object` method; it must be called while holding that object's monitor, it releases the monitor while waiting, and it ends on notify, interrupt or timeout.

### Deadlock

A **deadlock** is a cycle of threads each waiting for a lock held by the next. All four conditions must hold: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption (locks cannot be taken away), and circular wait. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. The classic cause is two threads taking two locks in opposite order. Here are two transfers between accounts, `A to B` and `B to A`, each locking "from" and then "to":

blocks.text: The `sleep(100)` simply makes the unlucky interleaving certain. With real code the same bug waits months for the right timing. Start it and attach `jstack` from a second terminal (get the pid with `jcmd -l`):

`jstack` detects monitor deadlocks for you and prints the cycle: thread t1 holds the account at `...80d8` and waits for `...8120`, thread t2 holds `...8120` and waits for `...80d8`. The line number points to the inner `synchronized (to)`. Without that summary, you would search for threads in state `BLOCKED (on object monitor)` with `waiting to lock` lines and follow the "held by" chain. A thread that is hung but is not part of a reported cycle is blocked for another reason (I/O, a lock-free spin, a stuck `wait`). Take two or three dumps a few seconds apart: threads that are in the same place in all of them are the ones stuck.

#### The cure: a global lock order

If every thread acquires locks in the same global order, no cycle can form. For two accounts, order by a unique id:

blocks.title: DeadlockFixed.java

blocks.code:
$ java DeadlockFixed.java
a=110 b=90
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: Both transfers now lock the lower-id account first. A transfer of 10 from a to b and of 20 from b to a nets a=110, b=90 and always terminates. Other strategies: acquire all locks at once through one coarser lock, use `tryLock` with a timeout (explicit locks, next chapter) and back off, or avoid holding one lock while calling code that takes another ("open calls"). Calling an overridable or callback method while holding a lock is a frequent hidden cause.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The `static long next` id counter in `DeadlockFixed` is itself not thread-safe; it is fine here because both accounts are created by `main` before any thread starts. In real code use an `AtomicLong`.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Production deadlocks usually involve one lock in your code and one in a framework or database: a request thread holds a synchronized cache lock and waits for a connection from an exhausted connection pool, while the thread holding the last connection waits for that cache lock. A thread dump shows both stacks immediately. Many production services capture `jstack` or `jcmd Thread.print` automatically when health checks fail.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Intrinsic locks in short.

- Every object is a monitor; `synchronized` gives mutual exclusion and a happens-before edge from unlock to the next lock of the same object.
- Only critical sections using the same lock object exclude each other; guard all reads and writes of shared state with one lock; prefer a private lock object.
- Monitors are reentrant. Keep critical sections short; never do I/O or call foreign code while holding a lock.
- Use `wait`/`notifyAll` in a `while` loop, holding the lock; wake-ups can be spurious or stolen.
- Deadlock needs a lock cycle. Prevent it with a global lock order; diagnose it with `jstack`.

The cheapest way to make shared data safe is to not share it, or to share it only when it can never change. This chapter covers those two strategies, and then the failure modes that remain even when your locking is correct: your threads can stop making progress.

### Do not share: thread confinement

An object that is only ever reachable from one thread needs no synchronisation. This is **thread confinement**, and it is the foundation of most safe concurrent code. There are three levels:

- **Stack confinement.** Local variables live on the thread's own stack. An object created in a method and never stored in a field or passed elsewhere is private to that thread. Primitive locals are always confined. This is why most of your code is already thread-safe.
- **Ad hoc confinement.** You *promise* by convention that only one thread touches the object (a Swing/JavaFX UI component touched only by the UI thread). The compiler cannot check it, so use it sparingly and document it.
- `ThreadLocal` **confinement.** Each thread gets its own copy of a variable, enforced by the library.

### ThreadLocal

A `ThreadLocal<T>` holds one value *per thread*. Under the hood each `Thread` object has a small map from `ThreadLocal` objects to values; `get()` and `set()` look up the current thread's map. Use cases:

1. **Per-thread instances of non-thread-safe helpers.** The classic example is `SimpleDateFormat`, which keeps parsing state in the object and corrupts output if shared (today you would use the immutable `DateTimeFormatter` instead).
2. **Implicit per-request context** that you do not want to pass through every method: a request id for logging, the current user, a transaction. (This is how Spring's transaction and security contexts reach deep code.)

blocks.title: Confine.java

blocks.code:
$ java Confine.java
t-a handling req-1, date 1970-01-01
t-b handling req-2, date 1970-01-01
main sees: null
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice: `ThreadLocal.withInitial` creates each thread's value lazily on first `get()`. The line order of `t-a` and `t-b` varies. `main` sees `null` because it never called `set`: the values are invisible to other threads. The `try`/`finally` with `remove()` is not decoration; it is the most important line.

#### ThreadLocal leaks in thread pools

Pool threads live as long as the application. If a task calls `set` and never `remove`, the value stays attached to that pool thread, long after the task ended. Two problems follow:

1. **Stale data bleeding between requests.** The next task on that thread calls `get()` and sees the previous request's user or transaction. This is a security bug, not just a leak.
2. **Memory leaks.** A value that references a large object graph (or a class loader, in an application server) is retained as long as the thread lives. After a web-app redeploy, the old class loader cannot be collected.

Always `remove()` in a `finally` when the thread is not yours. Prefer to avoid `ThreadLocal` for passing data when an explicit parameter works: hidden state makes code harder to test and reason about. Also note `InheritableThreadLocal` copies the parent's value into a child thread at creation, which interacts badly with pools (the value is copied once, when the pool creates the thread, not per task).

Virtual threads (Java 21, a later chapter) support `ThreadLocal`, but a program can have millions of virtual threads, so a per-thread cache of heavy objects becomes expensive. Java 25 finalised **scoped values** (JEP 506), an immutable, bounded-lifetime alternative for passing context to called code and child tasks; it is designed with virtual threads and structured concurrency in mind. (Scoped values are not available on Java 21 without preview, so we do not run an example here.)

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: In an application server or any pool, a `ThreadLocal` without `remove()` is a bug waiting for load. If you see `ThreadLocal` in code review, look for the `remove()` call.

### Do not mutate: immutability

An **immutable** object never changes state after construction. All its fields are set once; nothing can see it half-built (given safe construction, see the final-field rule of the memory model chapter). Immutable objects are thread-safe by construction, without locks: any number of threads can read them, and they can be shared and cached freely. `String`, the boxed numbers, `BigDecimal`, `java.time` types, records of immutable components and `List.of(...)` are all immutable.

The checklist for an immutable class:

1. Declare the class `final` (or make constructors private), so no subclass can add mutable state.
2. Make all fields `private final`.
3. Do not provide setters or any method that changes state.
4. Make **defensive copies** of mutable inputs in the constructor and of mutable outputs in getters (or store unmodifiable collections).
5. Do not let `this` escape from the constructor.

blocks.title: Immutable.java

blocks.code:
$ java Immutable.java
[book, pen]
read-only
Point[x=1, y=2]
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
`List.copyOf(items)` takes a snapshot: the later `src.add("laptop")` does not leak into the order, and the list the order exposes rejects modification. A record such as `Point` is *shallowly* immutable: its fields are final, but if a component is a mutable object (for example an `ArrayList`) the record is not deeply immutable. Immutability costs allocation when you "change" something (you create a new object), but modern allocation and garbage collection are cheap, and the safety is usually well worth it.

#### Thread-safety strategies at a glance

rows: Only one thread ever sees the data
One thread at a time touches the data
Hand data over, then stop touching it
blocks.caption: Strategies for sharing state.

blocks.text:
Pick them in this order: confine if possible; make immutable if possible; otherwise lock or use a ready-made concurrent class.

### Liveness problems

A program is **safe** if nothing bad happens (no corrupted data) and **live** if something good eventually happens (work gets done). Locks buy safety, and each one adds a risk to liveness. We already met deadlock. The three classic liveness failures:

#### Deadlock

Threads wait on each other in a cycle and none can proceed. All four Coffman conditions must hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait. Prevention: lock ordering, a single coarse lock, `tryLock` with timeouts. Detection: `jstack` or `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` for monitors and ownable synchronizers. Deadlocks are not limited to locks: a thread pool whose tasks wait for other tasks submitted to the same (full) pool can deadlock too ("thread-starvation deadlock"), for example a fixed pool of 2 threads where both tasks block waiting for subtasks that are queued behind them.

#### Livelock

Threads are not blocked; they are busy reacting to each other and make no progress. The standard picture is two people in a corridor, each stepping aside in the same direction, repeatedly. In code, two threads that each take a lock, fail to get the second lock with `tryLock`, release the first, and retry immediately in lock-step can livelock. The remedy is **randomised backoff**: sleep a random short time before retrying, which breaks the symmetry. A livelock burns CPU, so in a dump the threads show RUNNABLE or TIMED\_WAITING and the CPU is high, which distinguishes it from a deadlock (BLOCKED, CPU idle).

#### Starvation

A thread is ready to run but never gets the resource it needs, because others keep taking it. Causes: a thread holding a lock for a very long time; a low-priority task behind a flood of high-priority ones; **unfair locks**. Intrinsic locks make no fairness promise, and neither does `ReentrantLock` by default, which allows *barging* (a new arrival may take the lock ahead of queued threads) because that is faster. `new ReentrantLock(true)` is fair (first come, first served) at a cost to throughput. Avoid long critical sections and let queues, not priorities, order work.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How can you avoid deadlock? Break one of its four conditions. The practical approaches: acquire locks in a fixed global order; hold as few locks as possible and for as short a time as possible; do not call foreign (overridable) code while holding a lock; use `tryLock` with a timeout and back off; and prefer higher-level constructs (concurrent collections, executors, immutable data) that avoid explicit locking. To diagnose, take a thread dump with `jstack`/`jcmd` `Thread.print`, which reports Java-level deadlocks.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between a deadlock and a livelock? In a deadlock the threads are blocked forever waiting for each other and use no CPU. In a livelock they keep running and responding to each other (retrying, backing off in lock-step) but make no progress, so CPU use is high.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Safe sharing comes before locking.

- Prefer confinement (locals, `ThreadLocal`) and immutability (final fields, defensive copies, records, `List.copyOf`) to locks.
- `ThreadLocal` needs `remove()` in `finally` on pooled threads, or values leak and bleed across requests.
- Liveness failures: deadlock (cycle, idle), livelock (busy, no progress), starvation (never scheduled or never gets the lock).
- Prevent deadlock with lock ordering, short critical sections and timeouts; diagnose with thread dumps.
- Java 25 scoped values (JEP 506) are the modern alternative to `ThreadLocal` for context passing.

The `synchronized` keyword is simple and safe, but it is a blunt tool. You cannot give up waiting for it, you cannot ask "is it free right now?", you cannot interrupt a thread that is blocked on it, and a monitor has exactly one wait set. The `java.util.concurrent.locks` package (Java 5) and the `java.util.concurrent.atomic` package give you finer instruments. This chapter covers both: explicit locks, which still block threads, and atomic variables, which usually do not block at all.

The rule of thumb for the whole chapter: **start with** `synchronized` **or a ready-made concurrent class; reach for a** `Lock` **only when you need one of its extra abilities; reach for atomics for a single shared variable.** A higher-level class from the next chapters (executors, concurrent collections) is better still.

### ReentrantLock

`ReentrantLock` is a mutual-exclusion lock with the same basic semantics as an intrinsic monitor (one owner at a time, reentrant), plus extras. Reentrant means the owning thread can lock again without deadlocking itself; the lock counts how many times it was taken and is free only when `unlock()` was called the same number of times.

The price of the extras is discipline. A monitor is released automatically at the end of the `synchronized` block, even on exceptions. A `Lock` is released only when you call `unlock()`. The idiom is non-negotiable: call `lock()` **before** the `try`, and `unlock()` in `finally`.

blocks.title: LockDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java LockDemo.java
balance = 150
hold count = 2
locked after unlocks? false
tryLock(100ms) = false
tryDeposit while held = false
tryDeposit after release = true
final balance = 160
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `lock()` sits before `try`. If `lock()` itself threw and you had put it inside the `try`, the `finally` would call `unlock()` on a lock you do not hold and throw `IllegalMonitorStateException`, hiding the original error.
- `getHoldCount()` shows reentrancy: two `lock()` calls need two `unlock()` calls.
- `tryLock(timeout, unit)` returns `false` instead of waiting forever. This is the practical cure for the deadlocks you saw in the liveness chapter: if you cannot get the second lock in time, release the first and retry or fail.

#### What a Lock can do that synchronized cannot

#### Fairness

`new ReentrantLock(true)` creates a **fair** lock: when the lock is released it goes to the thread that has waited longest. The default is **non-fair**: a thread that calls `lock()` just as the lock is released may "barge" in front of queued threads. That sounds unjust, but it is faster, because the queued thread must be woken up, which takes microseconds, while the running thread can take the lock at once. Fair locks cost noticeably less throughput under contention. Use them only if you have observed starvation. Note that fairness of the lock does not guarantee fair thread scheduling, and the untimed `tryLock()` ignores fairness (it barges even on a fair lock).

### Condition: many wait sets per lock

A monitor has one wait set, used by `wait/notify`. In a bounded buffer that single set is shared by producers waiting for space and consumers waiting for items, so you must use `notifyAll()` and wake everyone. A `Condition` is created from a lock with `lock.newCondition()`, and one lock can have several. `await()`, `signal()` and `signalAll()` correspond to `wait()`, `notify()` and `notifyAll()`, and as with monitors you must hold the lock when you call them.

blocks.code:
$ java BoundedBuffer.java
consumed sum = 500500 (expected 500500)
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: The two rules from the monitor chapter carry over unchanged. First, always `await()` in a `while` loop that rechecks the condition, because of spurious wakeups and because another thread may have consumed the item between the signal and your wake-up. Second, `await()` releases the lock while it waits and re-acquires it before returning. With two conditions a producer only ever wakes consumers and vice versa, so `signal()` (one thread) is enough here. In real code you will rarely hand-write this; `ArrayBlockingQueue` (later in this Part) is exactly this class, already tested.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Do not call `wait()`/`notify()` on a `Lock` or `Condition` object. `Condition` is an ordinary object, so it also has the `Object.wait()` and `notify()` methods. Calling them compiles, but they use the object's own monitor, not the lock. The real methods are `await()` and `signal()`. If you see `IllegalMonitorStateException` from a `Condition`, check which one you called.

### ReadWriteLock

Many data structures are read far more often than they are written. A plain lock makes readers wait for each other for no reason. A `ReadWriteLock` has two locks: the **read lock** can be held by any number of threads as long as nobody holds the write lock, and the **write lock** is exclusive. `ReentrantReadWriteLock` is the standard implementation.

blocks.title: RwDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java RwDemo.java
book = 499
read locks held = 2
downgraded: write locked = false, readers = 1
upgrade with tryLock succeeded? false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- Two read locks were held at the same time (`read locks held = 2`). That is the whole benefit.
- **Downgrading** (write lock, then take the read lock, then release the write lock) is supported. It lets you update data and then read it consistently without a window where another writer sneaks in.
- **Upgrading** (holding a read lock and asking for the write lock) is not supported. With a blocking `writeLock().lock()` the thread would wait for all readers to leave, including itself, so it deadlocks. Release the read lock first, take the write lock, and recheck your condition, since the world may have changed in between.

A read-write lock is not automatically faster. Locking costs more than a plain lock, so it pays off only when reads dominate, the read section is not tiny, and there is real contention. Measure before you adopt it. For a map shared between threads, `ConcurrentHashMap` is almost always the better answer than a `HashMap` behind a read-write lock.

### StampedLock

`StampedLock` (Java 8) adds a third mode, the **optimistic read**: you read without locking, then check afterwards whether any write happened. If not, you got a consistent snapshot for free. If a write did happen, you retry or fall back to a real read lock. Each lock acquisition returns a `long` **stamp** that you pass back to release or validate.

blocks.title: StampedDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java StampedDemo.java
distance = 5.0
valid before write? true
valid after write?  false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: The pattern in `distanceFromOrigin` is the one to memorise: take the stamp, copy fields into **local variables**, call `validate(stamp)`, and use only the locals. Between the copy and the validation the fields may be half-updated (a torn pair of `x` and `y`), but if validation succeeds, no write intervened, so the copies were consistent.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: StampedLock is not reentrant and has no Conditions. Locking the same `StampedLock` twice from one thread (for example a write lock followed by another write lock) deadlocks, because it does not track owners. Stamps are not tied to threads, so any thread can release with the stamp. It is also easy to misuse: forgetting to validate, or using fields after a failed validation. Use it for small, hot, read-mostly classes like the `Point` above, and prefer simpler tools elsewhere.

### Atomic variables and compare-and-swap

Consider `count++` on a shared `int`. It is three steps (read, add, write), so two threads can both read 7 and both write 8, losing an update. You saw the fix with `synchronized`. Modern CPUs offer a cheaper primitive: **compare-and-swap** **(CAS)**, a single indivisible instruction that says "set this memory location to NEW only if it currently holds EXPECTED, and tell me whether it worked". In Java it is exposed as `compareAndSet(expected, new)`.

The classes in `java.util.concurrent.atomic` wrap a single variable with CAS-based operations: `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `AtomicBoolean`, `AtomicReference<V>`, plus arrays (`AtomicIntegerArray`), and field updaters. Their reads and writes have `volatile` semantics, so they also give visibility and ordering.

The usage pattern is a **CAS loop**: read the current value, compute the new value, try to CAS, and if another thread got there first, loop and recompute. Nobody ever blocks, so a stalled thread cannot hold others up; this style is called **lock-free**.

blocks.title: CasDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java CasDemo.java
CAS 5->6: true, value 6
CAS 5->7: false, value 6
updateAndGet(x*10) = 60
accumulateAndGet(max with 3) = 60
max = 3999
cba null
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `compareAndSet(5, 7)` returned `false` because the value was already 6. A failed CAS is normal, not an error: it means "someone else changed it first".
- Prefer the built-in loops: `updateAndGet(fn)`, `getAndUpdate(fn)`, `accumulateAndGet(x, fn)`, `incrementAndGet()`. The function you pass must be **side-effect free**, because it can run more than once when the CAS fails.
- `updateMax` and the `Stack` show the shape of every lock-free algorithm: snapshot, compute, CAS, retry. The stack's `push` creates a new immutable `Node` each time; immutability is what makes the CAS safe.

#### Atomics versus synchronized versus volatile

Now the race from the memory-model chapter, measured with four threads of 500,000 increments each:

blocks.title: CounterRace.java

blocks.code:
$ java CounterRace.java
expected      = 2000000
plain int     correct? false
volatile int  correct? false
synchronized  = 2000000
AtomicLong    = 2000000
LongAdder     = 2000000
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Both the plain and the `volatile` counters lose updates (the exact counts differ on every run, so the program only prints whether the result was correct; it was not). `volatile` fixes visibility, not atomicity: `vol++` is still read-modify-write. `synchronized`, `AtomicLong` and `LongAdder` are all exact.

#### LongAdder: atomics under heavy contention

When many threads hammer one `AtomicLong`, they all spin on CAS against the same memory location, and most attempts fail and retry. `LongAdder` (Java 8) avoids this by keeping a **set of cells**: under contention each thread updates a different cell, and `sum()` adds the cells up on demand. `increment()` is much cheaper under contention, at the price of a `sum()` that is not a single atomic snapshot and extra memory. Use `LongAdder` (or `LongAccumulator` for max/min) for statistics counters such as request counts and metrics that are written often and read rarely. Use `AtomicLong` when you need the exact current value atomically, for example to generate unique IDs with `incrementAndGet()`.

#### The ABA problem

CAS asks "is the value still A?". If another thread changed it A to B and back to A, the CAS succeeds although the world changed. For a counter that is harmless. For a linked structure it can be fatal: a node may have been popped, reused and pushed again, so your idea of what `next` points to is stale. In Java, garbage collection removes the commonest form of the bug (a node cannot be recycled while you still hold a reference to it), but it can still appear with values, or with pooled and reused objects. `AtomicStampedReference` pairs the reference with an `int` stamp (a version number) and CASes both; `AtomicMarkableReference` pairs it with a boolean flag.

blocks.title: AbaDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java AbaDemo.java
plain CAS succeeds despite A-B-A: true
stamped CAS succeeds: false, stamp now 2
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The plain CAS "succeeded" although the value had changed twice. The stamped version failed, correctly, because the stamp had moved from 0 to 2.

#### Under the hood

Atomics are implemented with `VarHandle` (Java 9, which replaced the internal `Unsafe` calls). On x86-64 a CAS compiles to a single `lock cmpxchg` instruction; on ARM, to a load-linked/store-conditional pair or a dedicated atomic instruction. You can use `VarHandle` directly for fine-grained control (`compareAndSet`, `getAcquire`, `setRelease`), but that is library-author territory. `AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater` and friends let you do CAS on a `volatile` field of another class when you cannot afford an `AtomicInteger` object per instance.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is CAS, and what is its downside compared with a lock? CAS is a single hardware instruction that atomically sets a variable to a new value only if it still holds the expected value. Atomic classes loop on it (read, compute, CAS, retry) so threads never block. Downsides: under heavy contention many CAS attempts fail and burn CPU (use `LongAdder`), it protects only one variable (a multi-field invariant needs a lock or an immutable snapshot in an `AtomicReference`), and it is exposed to the ABA problem (use `AtomicStampedReference`).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Is `volatile int count; count++` thread-safe? No. `volatile` guarantees that writes are visible and ordered, but `count++` is three operations (read, add, write), so two threads can interleave and lose an update. Use `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` or `synchronized`.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In a Spring Boot service you rarely write `ReentrantLock` yourself. You meet atomics in metrics counters (Micrometer uses `LongAdder`-style counters), in ID generators, and in "run once" flags (`AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false,` `true)`). Locks appear inside libraries: connection pools, caches and `ConcurrentHashMap` itself.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Explicit locks and atomics are the toolbox beyond `synchronized`.

- `ReentrantLock`: `lock()` before `try`, `unlock()` in `finally`; extras are `tryLock`, `lockInterruptibly`, fairness and multiple `Condition`s. Default is non-fair, which is faster.
- `ReadWriteLock` helps only when reads dominate; downgrading works, upgrading deadlocks. `StampedLock` adds optimistic reads but is non-reentrant and easy to misuse.
- CAS is one atomic instruction; atomic classes build lock-free CAS loops. Pass side-effect-free functions to `updateAndGet`.
- `volatile` is not atomic for `x++`. Use `AtomicLong`, or `LongAdder` for write-heavy counters.
- ABA is real for reference-based structures; `AtomicStampedReference` adds a version.

Creating a `new Thread` per task is the first thing every beginner does, and the first thing that breaks in production. A platform thread reserves memory for its stack (typically up to 1 MB of address space), costs microseconds to start, and the operating system can only schedule so many of them. A burst of 50,000 requests becomes 50,000 threads, and the machine dies of memory pressure and context switching long before the work is done.

The fix is to **separate the task from how it runs**. You describe the work as a `Runnable` or `Callable`, and hand it to an **executor**, which owns a small pool of reusable worker threads. The pool bounds resource use, removes thread start-up cost from the request path, and gives you a single place to configure queueing, rejection, naming and shutdown. This is the Executor framework (Java 5), the workhorse of server-side Java before virtual threads and still the right tool for CPU-bound work and for bounding concurrency.

### The interfaces

Three interfaces form a ladder.

- `Executor` has one method, `void execute(Runnable)`. It decouples submission from execution policy.
- `ExecutorService` adds lifecycle (`shutdown`, `shutdownNow`, `awaitTermination`, `close`) and task submission that returns a `Future`: `submit`, `invokeAll`, `invokeAny`.
- `ScheduledExecutorService` adds delayed and periodic tasks.

`Runnable` returns nothing and cannot throw a checked exception. `Callable<V>` returns a `V` and may throw `Exception`. A `Future<V>` is a handle to a result that may not exist yet: `get()` blocks until it does, `get(timeout, unit)` gives up, `cancel(mayInterrupt)` tries to stop the task, `isDone()` and `isCancelled()` report state. Behind the scenes `submit` wraps your task in a `FutureTask`, which is both a `Runnable` (the pool runs it) and a `Future` (you wait on it).

blocks.title: PoolBasics.java

blocks.code:
$ java PoolBasics.java
order 1 -> 20
order 2 -> 40
order 3 failed: java.lang.IllegalStateException: order 3 is invalid
order 4 -> 80
timed out, cancelling: true
isCancelled = true, isDone = true
A B C <- invokeAll keeps submission order
invokeAny returned one of A/B/C: true

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- A task's exception does not escape on the worker thread. It is stored in the `Future` and re-thrown by `get()` wrapped in an `ExecutionException`; the real failure is `getCause()`. Order 3 failed while orders 1, 2 and 4 were unaffected.
- `get(100, MILLISECONDS)` throws `TimeoutException`, but the task keeps running unless you call `cancel(true)`, which interrupts the worker. The task must respond to interruption (here `Thread.sleep` does) for the cancel to take effect quickly.
- `invokeAll` waits for all tasks and returns futures in the order of the input list. `invokeAny` returns the result of one task that completed successfully and cancels the rest.
- `shutdown()` is in a `finally`. A pool whose threads are non-daemon keeps the JVM alive until it is shut down.

### Inside ThreadPoolExecutor

Every standard pool is a `ThreadPoolExecutor` configured with seven parameters. Understanding them is the difference between a pool that behaves and one that deadlocks the service at 2 a.m.

The order of decisions on each `execute(task)` is the single most important fact about the class:

1. If fewer than `corePoolSize` threads are running, start a new thread and give it this task (even if other core threads are idle).
2. Otherwise try to put the task in the queue. If that works, a worker will pick it up.
3. If the queue refuses (it is full), and fewer than `maximumPoolSize` threads exist, start a new non-core thread.
4. Otherwise the pool is saturated: call the rejection handler.

Notice what this means: **the pool grows beyond the core size only after the queue is full.** With an unbounded queue (the default of `newFixedThreadPool`) step 3 never happens, so `maximumPoolSize` is irrelevant. The demonstration below uses core 2, max 4 and a queue of capacity 2, and keeps every task blocked on a latch so you can watch the state evolve (the `active` count is read while workers are starting, so it can occasionally lag by one; the pool sizes and queue lengths are the point).

task 2 accepted: pool=2 active=2 queued=0
