Task 7 finds a full queue and a full pool: with `AbortPolicy` it throws `RejectedExecutionException`, with `DiscardPolicy` it silently vanishes (note the count of completed tasks is 6 in both runs). Silent loss is rarely what you want.

### Queues

The queue choice defines the pool's behaviour more than any other parameter.

rows: Never full, so the pool never grows past the core size and never rejects. Under overload the queue grows until `OutOfMemoryError`. Used by `newFixedThreadPool` and `newSingleThreadExecutor`.
Bounded. Gives back-pressure: when full, the pool grows to the maximum, then rejects. The usual production choice.

Capacity zero: a hand-off. Every task needs a free worker or a new thread. Used by `newCachedThreadPool` (core 0, max `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, 60 s keep-alive), which can create thousands of threads under load.
Unbounded, ordered tasks (tasks must be `Comparable`). Not FIFO. Beware submit-wrapped tasks, which are `FutureTask`s, not your comparable class.
Elements become available after a delay; the basis of scheduled pools.
blocks.caption: Work queues and what they do to a pool.

blocks.text:
### Rejection policies

When the queue is full and the pool is at its maximum, the `RejectedExecutionHandler` decides:

- `AbortPolicy` (default): throw `RejectedExecutionException`. The caller learns about overload immediately. Often the right choice, because you can convert it into an HTTP 503.
- `CallerRunsPolicy`: the submitting thread runs the task itself. This is built-in **back-pressure**: while the caller is busy running a task it cannot submit more, so the producer slows down to the speed of the consumers.
- `DiscardPolicy`: silently drop the new task. Dangerous.
- `DiscardOldestPolicy`: drop the oldest queued task and retry. Also loses work silently.
- A custom handler: log, count a metric, or block with `queue.put`.

blocks.title: CallerRunsDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java CallerRunsDemo.java
task B ran on: main
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: Task B ran on `main`, the submitting thread, because the only worker was busy and the hand-off queue could not hold it.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: CallerRunsPolicy can run tasks on a thread that must not block. If the submitter is an event-loop or request-accepting thread, running a slow task on it stalls everything that thread does. And if the submitter is itself a worker of the same pool, you get unexpected recursion. Know who calls `submit` before choosing it.

### The factory methods and why teams ban them

`Executors` offers shortcuts:

rows: Unbounded queue: memory exhaustion, unbounded latency under overload.
Unbounded thread creation: `unable to create` `native thread`.
Same unbounded queue; tasks run strictly in order.
Periodic task that throws is cancelled silently.
a new virtual thread per task
No limit on concurrency; bound external resources yourself.
Daemon threads; for many small independent tasks.
blocks.caption: Executors factory methods.

blocks.text:
The well-known Alibaba Java guidelines and several style guides forbid `newFixedThreadPool` and `newCachedThreadPool` in production code for exactly the two hidden risks above. The remedy is to construct `ThreadPoolExecutor` directly with a **bounded queue**, an explicit **rejection policy**, and a **named thread factory**. For learning code and short-lived tools the factories are perfectly fine.

### Sizing a pool

There is no magic number, but there is a method.

- **CPU-bound work** (parsing, hashing, computation) never waits: more threads than cores only add context switching. Start with `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()` (or cores + 1).
- **I/O-bound work** (database, HTTP calls) spends most of its time waiting, so more threads keep the CPUs busy. A classical estimate is `threads = cores × (1 + wait time / compute time)`. If a task computes 10 ms and waits 90 ms, that is about 10 times the core count.
- **Little's law** is a good cross-check: concurrent requests in the system = arrival rate × average time in the system. If you serve 200 requests per second and each takes 50 ms, about 10 are in flight at any moment, so a pool of 10 to 20 is plenty.
- Mix workloads in one pool and a slow dependency can starve fast work. Use **separate pools** (bulkheads) for different downstream systems.
- Verify with measurements under realistic load, and watch `getQueue().size()`, `getActiveCount()` and rejection counts.

Also remember that a pool size is not your real limit. If the database allows 20 connections, a 200-thread pool only moves the waiting from the queue to the connection pool.

### Shutdown

A pool must be shut down, or its non-daemon workers keep the JVM running forever.

- `shutdown()`: stop accepting tasks; already submitted ones (running and queued) finish. Returns immediately.
- `shutdownNow()`: stop accepting, try to cancel running tasks by interrupting their threads, and return the list of tasks that never started.
- `awaitTermination(time, unit)`: block until the pool has terminated or the time passes.
- `close()` (Java 19+): calls `shutdown()` and waits for termination (it interrupts the thread via `shutdownNow` if the waiting thread is interrupted). This lets you use `ExecutorService` in try-with-resources.

blocks.title: ShutdownDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java ShutdownDemo.java
isShutdown = true, isTerminated = false
submit after shutdown -> RejectedExecutionException
task 1 finished normally
task 2 (was queued)
terminated in time = true
long task interrupted by shutdownNow
never started: 0
try-with-resources waits for this task
after close()
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The recipe in the middle (shutdown, wait a grace period, then `shutdownNow`, then wait again) is the standard graceful-then-forceful shutdown. Running tasks only stop if they react to interruption, so write long tasks to check `Thread.interrupted()` or call blocking methods that throw `InterruptedException`.

### Scheduled executors

`ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor` runs tasks after a delay or periodically. Three methods matter:

- `schedule(task, delay, unit)`: run once.
- `scheduleAtFixedRate(task, initialDelay, period, unit)`: runs at `start, start+period, start+2*period...`. If a run takes longer than the period, the next run starts late, but runs never overlap.
- `scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, initialDelay, delay, unit)`: waits `delay` after each run **finishes**. Use it when you want a pause between runs rather than a steady rate.

blocks.title: SchedDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java SchedDemo.java
one-shot ran
tick 1
tick 2
ticks = 2, periodic.isDone() = true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The periodic task threw on its second run and **was never run again**, silently: `isDone()` became `true` and no error was printed. For periodic tasks, wrap the body in `try/catch (Throwable)` and log, unless you really want a failure to stop the schedule. For anything calendar-like (cron expressions, "every day at 02:00") use a scheduler library or Spring's `@Scheduled`, not a raw `Timer` (single thread, one failure kills it).

### Common mistakes

#### 1. Swallowed exceptions

`submit()` captures a task's exception in its `Future`; if nobody calls `get()`, you never see it. `execute()` lets the exception propagate to the thread's uncaught-exception handler, and the pool replaces the dead worker. This program shows both, using a custom `ThreadFactory` to name the threads and to install a handler:

blocks.title: ExecMistakes.java

blocks.code:
$ java ExecMistakes.java
1. submit() with a failing task:
  nothing was printed; the exception waits inside the Future
  get() throws: java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom
2. execute() with a failing task:
  handler on billing-1: java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom 2
3. pool keeps working on: billing-2
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Note that the replacement worker is `billing-2`: the thread that died with the exception was `billing-1`. Always give pool threads meaningful names; they are what you will read in thread dumps and logs.

#### 2. Blocking on a Future from inside the same pool

A task that submits a subtask to its own pool and calls `get()` holds a worker while waiting for a worker. With a pool of N threads and N such parents, nothing can run: **thread-pool deadlock** (also called thread starvation deadlock, shown in the liveness chapter). Use separate pools, a larger pool, or `CompletableFuture` chaining (next chapter).

#### 3. ThreadLocal and context leaking through pool threads

Workers are reused, so `ThreadLocal` values set by one task are still there for the next. Always `remove()` in `finally`, as covered in the confinement chapter.

#### 4. Forgetting to shut down, or shutting down the shared pool

Create the pool once, share it, and shut it down in one place (for example a `@PreDestroy` method or a JVM shutdown hook). Creating a new pool per request is the same mistake as creating a thread per request, only slower.

#### 5. Unbounded everything

`newFixedThreadPool` plus an unbounded queue plus a slow downstream service is the classic outage: tasks pile up, memory climbs, latency becomes minutes, and the first symptom you see is `OutOfMemoryError`. Bound the queue and decide what the system does when full.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Explain what happens when you submit a task to a ThreadPoolExecutor. If fewer than `corePoolSize` threads exist, a new thread is started for the task. Otherwise the task is offered to the queue. If the queue is full and fewer than `maximumPoolSize` threads exist, a new thread is started. If both are full, the `RejectedExecutionHandler` runs (default: throw `RejectedExecutionException`). Corollary: with an unbounded queue the pool never grows past the core size, so `maximumPoolSize` is ignored.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is `Executors.newFixedThreadPool` discouraged in production? It uses an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue`, so under overload tasks accumulate until memory runs out, and there is no back-pressure or rejection. Build a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a bounded queue, a rejection policy and a named `ThreadFactory`.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Boot hides this. `@Async` uses a `TaskExecutor` (Boot auto-configures a `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` named `applicationTaskExecutor`) whose core size, max size and queue capacity are properties (`spring.task.execution.pool.*`). The same three-step growth rule applies: with Boot's default unbounded queue capacity, the pool will not grow past its core size. Tomcat's request pool (`server.tomcat.threads.max`, default 200) is also a thread pool, and it is why a slow database makes the whole service unresponsive.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Executors turn threads into a managed, bounded resource.

- Prefer executors to raw `Thread`s. Describe work as `Runnable`/`Callable`, wait with `Future`, and always shut the pool down.
- `ThreadPoolExecutor` order: core threads, then queue, then up to max threads, then reject. An unbounded queue means the pool never exceeds the core size.
- In production use a bounded queue, an explicit rejection policy (`AbortPolicy` or `CallerRunsPolicy`) and a named `ThreadFactory`.
- Size by workload: CPU-bound near the core count, I/O-bound larger; separate pools for separate dependencies.
- Exceptions hide in `submit()` Futures and kill periodic schedules silently; handle them deliberately.

A plain `Future` has a blocking design: to use the result you must call `get()` and park a thread until it is ready. Chain three remote calls with `Future` and you hold three threads hostage in turn, or you write nested callbacks by hand. `CompletableFuture` (Java 8) fixes this. It is a `Future` whose result you can also *continue from*: "when this finishes, do that", "when both of these finish, combine them", "if this fails, use a fallback". You build a pipeline of stages, much as the Streams chapters built pipelines of operations, and no thread waits while the stages are pending.

It also implements `CompletionStage`, the interface that defines all the chaining methods, and it is a **promise**: you can create an empty one with `new CompletableFuture<>()` and complete it later from anywhere with `complete(value)` or `completeExceptionally(error)`. That is how adapters turn callback-style APIs into futures.

blocks.text:
### Starting a computation

- `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier<T>)` runs a task that returns a value, in the common pool.
- `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier<T>, Executor)` runs it in **your** executor. This is what you should normally use (see the pitfalls below).
- `runAsync(Runnable)` is the no-result variant.
- `completedFuture(value)` and `failedFuture(ex)` (Java 9) create already-finished futures; useful for tests and for short-circuiting.

### Transforming and chaining

The method names follow a pattern: what the stage does to the previous result, and whether it runs on the thread that completed the previous stage or is handed to an executor (`...Async`).

rows: Consume the value (end of the chain).
Run an action ignoring the value.
Recover or transform: sees both outcomes.
blocks.caption: The chaining methods.

blocks.text: The most common beginner confusion is `thenApply` versus `thenCompose`. If your function returns a plain value, use `thenApply`. If it returns another `CompletableFuture` (it makes an async call), use `thenCompose`; `thenApply` would give you a `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>`, a nested future you then have to unwrap.

blocks.title: CfBasics.java

blocks.code:
$ java CfBasics.java
price: 4.0
composed: 300 / in stock
lamp 400 rated 4.5
allOf: 400, in stock, 4.5
three 100 ms calls took less than 250 ms: true
anyOf -> fast
all prices: [100, 200, 300]
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `price(...).thenApply(...)` returns immediately; the transformations run when the price arrives. The `join()` at the end is where the demo finally blocks, and in an application you would normally return the future to the caller instead.
- `thenCombine` runs the two calls **concurrently** and merges when both are done. Writing `price(...).thenCompose(p` `-> rating(...))` instead would run them one after the other. Use `thenCompose` only when the second call needs the first result.
- `allOf` returns `CompletableFuture<Void>`, so you read each individual future afterwards with `join()` (cheap, they are already complete). The last block shows the idiom to turn a `List<CompletableFuture<T>>` into a `CompletableFuture<List<T>>`.
- Three 100 ms calls finished in well under 250 ms, because they overlapped. Sequentially it would be 300 ms.
- `anyOf` returns `Object`, so you cast. It also completes with the first *completion*, even if that first completion is a failure.

### Which thread runs each stage?

This matters for performance and for correctness. A stage created with `thenApply` runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage, or, **if that stage is already complete when you attach the new one, on the calling thread**. The `...Async` variants always submit the step to an executor (the common pool unless you pass one).

blocks.title: CfThreads.java

blocks.code:
$ java CfThreads.java
cpus = 2, common pool parallelism = 1
supplyAsync (default executor) ran on: Thread-0
thenApply on completed future ran on: main
thenApplyAsync(.., ex) ran on: my-pool
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Typical output on a 2-CPU build machine (names and parallelism depend on your machine). Two things to read here. First, `thenApply` on a finished future ran on `main`: harmless for a cheap transformation, but a surprise if the step is slow and you thought it ran in the background. Second, with `supplyAsync` and no executor the thread is called `Thread-0`, not `ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1`. The reason: `CompletableFuture` uses the common `ForkJoinPool` only when its parallelism is greater than 1; on machines (or containers) with one or two CPUs, the common pool has parallelism 1 (here, `cpus - 1`), and `CompletableFuture` falls back to creating a **new thread per task**. So the same code behaves differently in a small container than on your laptop.

### Errors

An exception thrown inside any stage completes that stage exceptionally, and the failure **propagates through every** **dependent stage** (they are skipped) until a stage handles it. Nothing is printed, nothing is thrown at the point of failure. If nobody calls `join()`/`get()` and nobody attaches a handler, the failure is silently lost, the same trap as a lost `Future` from `submit`.

Wrapping rules: `get()` throws the checked `ExecutionException`; `join()` throws the unchecked `CompletionException`; both carry the original exception as `getCause()`. Inside `handle`, `exceptionally` and `whenComplete`, the `Throwable` you receive is often already wrapped in a `CompletionException` (it is for failures coming from a previous stage), so unwrap it if you test its type.

blocks.title: CfErrors.java

blocks.code:
$ java CfErrors.java
join() threw CompletionException, cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: pricing service down
get()  threw ExecutionException,  cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: pricing service down
exceptionally -> -1
handle -> failed: CompletionException / pricing service down
whenComplete saw: CompletionException
still failed afterwards: pricing service down
completeOnTimeout -> default
orTimeout -> TimeoutException
isCompletedExceptionally = true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `handle` and `whenComplete` both received a `CompletionException`, not the `IllegalStateException`: that is the wrapping. `ex.getCause()` is the real error. A common helper: `Throwable root = ex instanceof` `CompletionException ? ex.getCause() : ex;`.
- `exceptionally` supplies a fallback value but cannot see the successful result. `handle` sees both. `whenComplete` is for side effects such as logging; the outcome continues unchanged, which is why the final `join()` still threw.
- `orTimeout` makes the future fail with `TimeoutException` after the delay; `completeOnTimeout` completes it normally with a default. Both are Java 9 additions. They do **not** stop the underlying work: the slow supplier keeps running. They only decide what the future reports. Likewise `cancel(true)` on a `CompletableFuture` does not interrupt the running task (the Javadoc says the flag has no effect), it only completes the future with `CancellationException`.
- Since Java 12 there are also `exceptionallyCompose` (recover with another async call) and `...Async` forms of `exceptionally`.

### Executors, the common pool and blocking

`supplyAsync(task)` without an executor uses the **common pool**, a single JVM-wide `ForkJoinPool` that is also used by parallel streams. It is sized for CPU-bound work (`cores - 1` threads). Three consequences:

1. **Never run blocking I/O in the common pool.** A few tasks waiting for a database or HTTP response occupy all the threads, and every parallel stream and every other `CompletableFuture` in the application stalls.
2. **Pass your own executor** for I/O (a bounded `ThreadPoolExecutor` per downstream dependency, or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` in Java 21+). It also makes thread names meaningful in dumps.
3. **Do not block a worker waiting for another stage that needs a worker.** Calling `join()` inside a task that runs on a small pool is the thread-pool deadlock from the executors chapter, in a new disguise:

blocks.title: CfStarve.java

blocks.code:
$ java CfStarve.java
blocking style: stuck (timed out after 500 ms)
composed style: 43
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The blocking version never finishes: the single worker is held by the outer task, which waits for an inner task queued for the same worker. The composed version needs no waiting thread, because `thenCompose` only *registers* the next step. (The worker in the demo is a daemon thread because a stuck `join()` ignores interrupts and would otherwise prevent the JVM from exiting.) This is the practical reason to prefer `thenCompose` to a nested `join()`.

#### Useful extras

- `delayedExecutor(delay, unit)` (Java 9) is an `Executor` that starts the task after a delay: `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS))` is a one-line retry back-off.
- `thenApplyAsync(fn, executor)`: hand a heavy transformation to a specific pool.
- `copy()` and `minimalCompletionStage()` (Java 9) give consumers a view they cannot complete or cancel.
- `join()` is the same as `get()` without checked exceptions; `getNow(default)` returns the default if not done; `isDone()`, `isCompletedExceptionally()`.
- `resultNow()` and `exceptionNow()` (Java 19, on `Future`) read a completed result without declared exceptions.

#### Design guidance

- Return `CompletableFuture<T>` from async service methods, and let the outermost caller decide when (or whether) to block.
- Always supply an executor for anything that is not pure CPU work.
- Attach an error handler at the end of every chain whose result nobody reads (fire-and-forget), or the failure vanishes.
- Put timeouts on remote calls (`orTimeout`), and decide what the fallback is.
- Keep stages small and side-effect free; for sequential-looking business logic with blocking calls, a virtual thread (later in this Part) often produces simpler code than a long chain of lambdas.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between thenApply and thenCompose? And thenCombine? `thenApply` maps the result with a function returning a plain value. `thenCompose` is for a function that itself returns a `CompletableFuture` (flat-map), keeping the chain flat. `thenCombine` joins two independent futures, running both concurrently and applying a function when both are done.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Which thread runs `supplyAsync` and its `thenApply`? `supplyAsync` without an executor runs in the common `ForkJoinPool` (or a new thread per task if the common pool's parallelism is 1). `thenApply` runs on the thread that completed the previous stage, or on the caller if the stage is already complete; `thenApplyAsync` submits to an executor.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring's `@Async` methods can return `CompletableFuture<T>`. Web clients and drivers expose callbacks or reactive types, which teams adapt to `CompletableFuture` with a promise (`new CompletableFuture<>()` completed in the callback). Fan-out "gather data from three services" endpoints are the standard use of `thenCombine` and `allOf`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
CompletableFuture composes asynchronous steps without blocking threads.

- `thenApply` maps, `thenCompose` flat-maps, `thenCombine` merges two independent futures, `allOf`/`anyOf` wait for many.
- Failures skip dependent stages until `exceptionally`, `handle` or `whenComplete`; `join` throws `CompletionException`, `get` throws `ExecutionException`.
- Pass your own executor for blocking work. The common pool is small, shared with parallel streams, and a thread per task if parallelism is 1.
- Do not `join()` inside a task running on a small pool; compose instead.
- `orTimeout`/`completeOnTimeout` change what the future reports, not whether the work keeps running.

`synchronized`, locks and atomics are the atoms of concurrency. Most real coordination problems, though, are molecules that come up again and again: "wait until all N workers are ready", "allow at most 10 threads in here", "hand work from producers to consumers", "count words from many threads". The `java.util.concurrent` package provides ready-made, heavily tested solutions. Use them before you invent your own with `wait/notify`: they are shorter, faster, and correct in the corner cases you would forget.

This chapter has two halves: **synchronizers**, which make threads wait for each other, and **concurrent collections**, which let threads share data structures safely.

### CountDownLatch: wait for N events

A `CountDownLatch` starts with a count. `countDown()` decrements it; `await()` blocks until it reaches zero. It is **one-shot**: the count never resets. Two classic uses are a **start gate** (count 1: workers wait for `countDown()` so they all begin together, useful in tests) and a **completion signal** (count N: the coordinator waits until N workers have finished).

### CyclicBarrier: wait for each other, repeatedly

A `CyclicBarrier(parties)` makes `parties` threads wait at `await()` until the last one arrives; then they are all released, an optional **barrier action** runs once, and the barrier resets for the next round. Use it for phased computations: all workers finish step 1 before any starts step 2. If any thread is interrupted or times out while waiting, the barrier breaks and the others get `BrokenBarrierException`.

finished after the latch   = 3
latch count now 0 (cannot be reset)
  -- barrier tripped

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `countDown()` is in a `finally`. If a worker threw before reaching it, `done.await()` would hang forever. This is the number one latch bug.
- The latch's count ends at 0 and stays there; to run the scenario again you need a new latch. The barrier tripped twice: once per round.
- Latch: threads wait for *events* (any thread may count down, waiters and counters can be different threads). Barrier: threads wait for *each other* (the same threads both arrive and wait).

### Semaphore: limit concurrent access

A `Semaphore` holds a number of **permits**. `acquire()` takes one (blocking if none), `release()` returns one. It limits how many threads are inside a section at once: a pool of 10 database connections, at most 5 concurrent downloads, a rate limiter. `new Semaphore(n, true)` is fair. `tryAcquire()` and `tryAcquire(timeout)` do not block forever. A semaphore with one permit is a lock, except that it is not owned: any thread may release, which is both its power and its danger.

### Phaser and Exchanger

`Phaser` is a more flexible barrier: parties can `register()` and `arriveAndDeregister()` while it runs, it supports many phases, and you can override `onAdvance` to run code at each phase boundary and to terminate. Use it when the number of participants changes (for example a recursive task that spawns subtasks, each registering as a party). For a fixed set of parties, `CyclicBarrier` is simpler.

`Exchanger<V>` is a rendezvous for exactly two threads: each calls `exchange(x)`, blocks until the other arrives, and gets the other's object. It is rare in applications; the textbook use is double-buffering (one thread fills a buffer while the other drains the previous one, then they swap).

tryAcquire(5) on 3 free permits: false

main got:  from-other

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Always release what you acquired, in `finally`. A semaphore permit that is not released after an exception leaks: after enough leaks every thread blocks at `acquire()` and the service is dead with no error message. Acquire before the `try`, release in `finally`, exactly as with locks. Do the same for `countDown()`.

### BlockingQueue: producer-consumer without wait/notify

A `BlockingQueue` is a queue with two extra behaviours: `take()` **blocks** when the queue is empty, and `put(x)` **blocks** when a bounded queue is full. That is the whole producer-consumer pattern in the data structure itself. The producers and consumers need no locks or conditions, and a bounded queue gives you **back-pressure** for free: if consumers are slow, producers are slowed down instead of memory filling up.

### ConcurrentHashMap in depth

`ConcurrentHashMap` (CHM) is the map you use when many threads read and write one map. It is not `Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())`, which puts a single lock around every method and serialises all threads. CHM allows reads without locking at all and lets writers to different parts of the table run in parallel.

#### How it works (Java 8 and later)

- The table is an array of bins, like `HashMap`, with the same hash spreading idea and the same tree-ification of long bins (a bin with 8 or more entries in a table of at least 64 becomes a red-black tree).
- **Reads (**`get`**) take no lock.** Table slots and node values are `volatile`, so a reader sees a consistent value for the entry.
- **Writes** to an empty bin use a CAS to insert the first node. Writes to a non-empty bin use `synchronized` on the **head** **node of that bin only**. Two writers to different bins never block each other. (Java 7 used 16 fixed lock "segments"; Java 8 replaced them with per-bin locking, which scales with the table size.)
- **Resizing** is cooperative: threads that find a resize in progress help move bins instead of waiting.
- **Size** is not stored in one field (that would be a contention hot spot). It is spread over counter cells, like `LongAdder`, and summed on demand, so `size()` is an estimate under concurrent updates; `mappingCount()` returns the same as a `long` and is preferred for huge maps.
- **Iterators are weakly consistent**: they never throw `ConcurrentModificationException`, and they reflect the map at some point at or after the iterator's creation, possibly including later updates.
- **No null keys or values.** With a plain `HashMap`, `get(k) == null` is ambiguous (absent, or mapped to null?) and you can disambiguate with `containsKey`. In a concurrent map that second call is a race: the answer may change between the two calls. Banning nulls removes the ambiguity.

#### Compound operations must be atomic operations

Each CHM method is atomic, but a *sequence* of them is not. `get` followed by `put` is a classic check-then-act race. Use the atomic compound methods: `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, `computeIfPresent`, `compute`, `merge`, `replace(k, old,` `new)`, `remove(k, v)`.

putIfAbsent second: 10
after compute: {pen=7}

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- The `get` + `put` version loses updates even though both methods are individually thread-safe: two threads read the same old value. `merge("hits", 1, Integer::sum)` performs the whole read-modify-write atomically for that key.
- `computeIfAbsent(k, k -> new LongAdder())` is the idiom for a concurrent multi-counter or multi-map (`computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>())` is **not** safe, because the `ArrayList` itself is not thread-safe; use a concurrent collection as the value).
- `putIfAbsent` returns the previous value, or `null` if the key was absent, so a `null` result means "I inserted it".
- The bulk operations (`forEach`, `reduceValues`, `search`, ...) take a **parallelism threshold**: the map size above which the work is spread over the common pool. `Long.MAX_VALUE` forces sequential execution, `1` allows maximum parallelism.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The function passed to compute/computeIfAbsent/merge runs while the bin is locked. Keep it short and quick. It must not touch the same map (no nested `map.compute` or `computeIfAbsent` on it): that can deadlock or throw `IllegalStateException: Recursive update`. Do not call slow I/O inside it; other writers to that bin wait.

### Other concurrent collections

- `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` **/** `ConcurrentLinkedDeque`: unbounded, non-blocking, lock-free queues built on CAS. `poll()` returns `null` when empty (there is no `take`). `size()` walks the list, so it is O(n) and approximate; use `isEmpty()`. Choose them when consumers poll in a loop with other work to do, not when they should sleep until data arrives (use a `BlockingQueue` then).
- `ConcurrentSkipListMap` **/** `ConcurrentSkipListSet`: the concurrent, sorted `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` equivalent (a skip list gives O(log n) without a global lock). Use them when you need ordering plus concurrency; a `TreeMap` cannot be made concurrent cheaply.
- `CopyOnWriteArrayList` **/** `CopyOnWriteArraySet`: every mutation copies the whole backing array; reads and iteration need no lock and iterate over an immutable **snapshot**. Excellent for **rarely modified, frequently read** lists such as listener registries or configuration. Terrible for lists that change often (each add is O(n)).

blocks.code:
$ java CowDemo.java
ArrayList: ConcurrentModificationException
a b c -> list is now [a, b, c, d]
iterator made before add('e') saw 4 elements; list has 5
snapshot iterator does not support remove()
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The `CopyOnWriteArrayList` loop added an element during iteration without error, but the loop did not see it (it printed `a b c`, not `d`): the iterator works on the snapshot taken when it was created. The snapshot iterator also cannot modify the list (`remove()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`).

#### Synchronized wrappers versus concurrent collections

`Collections.synchronizedList/Map/...` wrap a collection so that each method takes one lock. That makes single calls thread-safe but still leaves compound actions and iteration unsafe (you must hold the wrapper's lock while iterating), and everything is serialised. The `java.util.concurrent` collections are designed for concurrency from the start: finer-grained locking or lock-free algorithms, iterators that tolerate modification, atomic compound methods. Prefer them. The legacy `Hashtable` and `Vector` are synchronised like the wrappers and are best left in the past.

#### Choosing

`Hand work to consumers, wait when empty`
blocks.caption: Which concurrent structure for which job.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety, and how is it different from Hashtable? `Hashtable` (and `synchronizedMap`) lock the whole map on every call. In Java 8+, `ConcurrentHashMap` reads without locks (volatile reads), inserts into an empty bin with a CAS, and otherwise synchronises only on the head node of the affected bin, so writes to different bins proceed in parallel. It forbids null keys and values, has weakly consistent iterators (no `ConcurrentModificationException`), and offers atomic compound operations (`merge`, `compute`, `putIfAbsent`). Java 7 used segment locks; Java 8 replaced them with per-bin locking.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: CountDownLatch versus CyclicBarrier? A latch is one-shot and event-based: waiters block until the count, decremented by anyone, reaches zero. A barrier is reusable and party-based: N threads wait for each other, are released together, and the barrier resets; it can run a barrier action when tripped.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: A Spring Boot application uses `ConcurrentHashMap` in many places without you seeing it: bean registries, caches, `Micrometer` meters. The idiom `cache.computeIfAbsent(key, this::load)` gives a "load once per key" cache, but a slow `load` blocks other writers to the same bin, which is why dedicated cache libraries (Caffeine) use their own design. `BlockingQueue` is the buffer in log appenders and in custom background workers.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Prefer the ready-made coordinators and collections to hand-written wait/notify.

- `CountDownLatch` (one-shot events), `CyclicBarrier` (reusable rendezvous), `Phaser` (dynamic parties), `Semaphore` (limit concurrency), `Exchanger` (swap between two threads). Release permits and count down in `finally`.
- `BlockingQueue` is producer-consumer in one object; bounded queues give back-pressure; poison pills stop consumers.
- `ConcurrentHashMap`: lock-free reads, per-bin writes, no nulls, weakly consistent iterators; use `merge`/`compute` instead of `get` + `put`.
- `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for read-mostly data; `ConcurrentSkipListMap` for sorted concurrent maps; `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` for non-blocking queues.

For two decades, Java servers faced an awkward choice. The natural way to write server code is **thread per request**: one thread handles one request from start to finish, calling blocking methods (database, HTTP, files) in plain sequential style. It is easy to read, easy to debug (the stack trace is the story of the request), and easy to profile. But a platform thread is an operating-system thread, and that costs memory (its stack), start-up time and scheduler work, so a server can afford only a few thousand of them. The throughput of such a server is capped by the number of threads, not by the CPU, even though most threads spend most of their time just *waiting* for I/O.

The industry answer was asynchronous programming: callbacks, `CompletableFuture` chains, reactive frameworks. They scale, but the code is harder to write, harder to debug (stack traces show the framework, not your logic), and virally changes every method signature.

**Virtual threads** (final in Java 21, JEP 444) give back the simple model. A virtual thread is a `Thread` that is managed by the JVM, not the operating system. It is so cheap that you create one per task, even millions, and when it blocks on I/O, it steps off its carrier thread and lets another virtual thread run. You write blocking code; the JVM makes it scale.

blocks.text:
### How they work

- **Carrier threads.** A virtual thread runs by being **mounted** on a platform thread called its carrier. The carriers are the threads of a dedicated `ForkJoinPool` (in FIFO mode), by default as many as there are CPUs (`jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism`, with a ceiling of `jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize`, 256 by default).
- **Unmounting.** When the virtual thread calls a blocking operation that the JDK has been adapted for (`Thread.sleep`, socket and file-channel I/O, `java.util.concurrent` locks, `BlockingQueue.take`, `Future.get`, and so on), the JVM copies the virtual thread's stack frames into a heap object, unmounts it, and the carrier immediately picks another runnable virtual thread. When the I/O completes, the virtual thread becomes runnable again and is mounted on *some* carrier (not necessarily the same one).
- **Cheap stacks.** The stack of a virtual thread lives on the heap as stack chunk objects and starts tiny, growing with the actual call depth. A platform thread reserves a fixed stack up front (typically about 1 MB of address space). That is the difference between thousands and millions of threads.
- **Preemption is not time-sliced.** The scheduler switches virtual threads when they block, not on a timer. A virtual thread in a tight CPU loop holds its carrier until it finishes. Virtual threads are for waiting, not for computing.

They are still real `java.lang.Thread` objects. `Thread.currentThread()`, `ThreadLocal`, interruption, `join`, thread dumps and debuggers all work. Existing blocking code runs unchanged.

### Creating them

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `Thread.ofVirtual().name("...").start(task)`, `Thread.startVirtualThread(task)`, and `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` are the three ways in. `Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(task)` gives a `Thread` in state `NEW` that you start yourself. There is also a `ThreadFactory` via `Thread.ofVirtual().factory()` for frameworks.
- Virtual threads are always **daemon** threads (they do not keep the JVM alive; `setDaemon(false)` is not allowed) and have an empty name unless you set one. Their priority is fixed.
- `ExecutorService` implements `AutoCloseable` since Java 19. The `try (ex)` block waits for all tasks at the end, so the timer around it measures real completion.
- The numbers (typical, measured on a 2-CPU build machine; yours will differ): 2000 tasks of 100 ms of blocking each took about 2 seconds on a pool of 100 platform threads (2000 / 100 × 100 ms) but about 0.13 seconds on virtual threads, which overlap all of them. The same code, a different executor.

### Thread per request, finally

The following program starts an HTTP server using only JDK classes (`com.sun.net.httpserver`), tells it to run each request on a new virtual thread, and then fires 300 concurrent requests from virtual threads. Each handler blocks for 200 ms. Written in the plain blocking style, with no callbacks.

blocks.title: VtServer.java

blocks.code:
$ java VtServer.java
300 of 300 requests answered by a virtual thread
each request blocks 200 ms; total 1324 ms (serial: 60000 ms)
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
300 requests, each blocking 200 ms, completed in well under a second (the printed time is typical and varies from run to run; serial execution would need 60 seconds). Every request was handled on a virtual thread. In a framework the setup is one line: in Spring Boot 3.2+, `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` makes the embedded server and the async executors use virtual threads.

### Rules for using virtual threads well

1. **Do not pool them.** A pool exists to ration an expensive resource; virtual threads are not expensive. Create one per task. If you want to *limit concurrency* (say, 20 calls into a rate-limited service), use a `Semaphore`, not a pool of virtual threads.
2. **Use them for blocking I/O-bound work**, not CPU-bound loops. For CPU-bound work a pool sized to the core count (or Fork/Join) is still right; virtual threads add nothing there.
3. **Keep code blocking and simple.** Do not wrap blocking calls in `CompletableFuture` just to make them "async"; a virtual thread already gives you that.
4. **Mind the resources behind the threads.** A million virtual threads can open a million connections; your database has a connection pool of 20. The pool becomes the bottleneck, which is how it should be, but make sure waiting there has a timeout.
5. **Prefer** `ReentrantLock` **and other** `java.util.concurrent` **tools** to `synchronized` around blocking calls on Java 21 (see pinning).

### Pinning

A virtual thread is **pinned** when it cannot unmount while blocked; it then holds its carrier hostage. In Java 21 the two causes are (1) blocking while inside a `synchronized` block or method, and (2) blocking in a native method or a foreign-function call. Pinning is not a correctness bug; the program works, but you lose scalability. Because there are only as many carriers as CPUs, a few pinned threads can stall the whole scheduler.

The program below runs eight virtual threads that each sleep 200 ms while holding a private lock (so there is no lock contention at all), once with `ReentrantLock` and once with `synchronized`. We limit the carriers to two with system properties set at the top of `main` (the command-line `-D` flags do the same):

blocks.title: VtPinning.java

blocks.code:
$ java VtPinning.java
8 virtual threads, each sleeps 200 ms, only 2 carrier threads
typical: with ReentrantLock  -> 215 ms
typical: with synchronized   -> 805 ms
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: With the `ReentrantLock`, a sleeping thread unmounts, so all eight overlap: about 200 ms. With `synchronized`, a sleeping thread keeps its carrier, so only two run at a time: 8 / 2 × 200 ms = about 800 ms. On Java 21 you can see the culprits with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short`, which printed lines like this during the synchronized run:

blocks.code:
$ java -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short VtPinning.java
VirtualThread[#30]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 reason:MONITOR
    VtPinning.lambda$run$0(VtPinning.java:20) <== monitors:1

blocks.text:
**Java 24 changed this.** JEP 491 (*Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning*, Java 24) lets a virtual thread that blocks inside `synchronized` release its carrier, so on Java 24 and 25 the second line above would be about as fast as the first. Pinning for native and foreign calls remains. (The listing and its output are Java 21 behaviour; the Java 24 change is described from the JEP and was not run here.) The practical consequences: on Java 21 audit libraries and your code for blocking calls inside `synchronized` (older JDBC drivers and some logging code were the usual suspects), and on 24+ you can mostly stop worrying. The JFR event `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` reports pinned blocking that lasts longer than a threshold.

### ThreadLocal and virtual threads

Virtual threads support `ThreadLocal`, including inheritance. It works, but think before using it. A `ThreadLocal` was designed for the world of few, long-lived, pooled threads, where caching an expensive object (a `SimpleDateFormat`, a buffer) in each thread is a good deal. With a million short-lived virtual threads each holding its own copy, the "cache" becomes a million copies. For **per-request context** (user, trace ID, transaction) prefer a parameter, or a `ScopedValue` (next chapter), which is immutable, automatically cleaned up and cheap. Never keep a `ThreadLocal` value that is large or that expects `remove()` to be called in a thread that gets reused: virtual threads are not reused, so the value simply dies with the thread, but the memory is held while it is alive.

### Observability

- **Thread dumps**: the classic `jstack` and `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` do *not* list virtual threads (there could be millions). Use `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file.json` to get a dump that includes them, grouped by their owner in structured-concurrency scopes.
- **JFR**: events `jdk.VirtualThreadStart`, `jdk.VirtualThreadEnd`, `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` and `jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed`.
- A debugger and stack traces work as for platform threads: the stack trace shows your own code path, one of the main wins over async styles.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What problem do virtual threads solve, and how do they differ from reactive programming? They remove the limit on the number of concurrent blocking tasks. Blocking calls unmount a virtual thread from its carrier, so a handful of OS threads can run millions of them, while code stays in simple sequential style with intact stack traces. Reactive programming achieves similar scalability by never blocking at all, at the price of callback/operator-chain code and awkward debugging. Virtual threads do not make CPU-bound code faster.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is pinning? A virtual thread is pinned when it blocks but cannot unmount, so it keeps occupying its carrier. In Java 21 this happens when blocking inside `synchronized` or in a native/foreign call. Java 24 (JEP 491) removed the `synchronized` case. Detect with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads` (21) or the `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` JFR event.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Boot 3.2 and later switch Tomcat and `@Async` to virtual threads with one property, `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`. The usual wins are services that spend their time waiting on databases and downstream HTTP calls. The usual surprises are a connection pool that becomes the true bottleneck, libraries that pin on Java 21, and monitoring tools that count platform threads.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Virtual threads make blocking code scale.

- A virtual thread (Java 21, JEP 444) is a JVM-managed `Thread` mounted on a few carrier threads; blocking operations unmount it so the carrier can run another.
- Create one per task with `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` or `Thread.ofVirtual()`. Never pool them; limit concurrency with a `Semaphore`.
- They help I/O-bound workloads; they do not speed up CPU-bound work and are not time-sliced.
- Pinning (blocking inside `synchronized` or native code) holds the carrier; fixed for `synchronized` in Java 24 (JEP 491). Use `ReentrantLock` on Java 21.
- Prefer parameters or `ScopedValue` to `ThreadLocal` for per-request context; use `jcmd Thread.dump_to_file` for dumps.
#### Concurrency Concepts

items.question: A program has three independent tasks and runs on a machine with one CPU core. Can it be concurrent? Can it be parallel?
items.answer: It can be concurrent (the OS or JVM time-slices the tasks), but not parallel: parallel execution needs at least two cores.

items.question: Name the three problems (the "big three") that make shared-memory threading hard.
items.answer: Atomicity (compound operations can interleave), visibility (writes may not be seen by other threads) and ordering (instructions can be reordered).

items.question: A job is 80 percent parallelisable. What is the maximum speed-up with unlimited cores? (Use the formula.)
items.answer: 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 5, so at most 5 times faster, no matter how many cores.

items.question: What is wrong with this reasoning: "my task is CPU-bound, so I will start 100 threads on my 4-core laptop to make it faster"?
items.answer: A CPU-bound task cannot use more than the 4 cores; the extra threads only add context-switch and memory overhead. The thread count should be about the number of cores.

items.question: What does this print, assuming `count` is a plain `int` field shared by two threads that each run the loop? `for (int i` `= 0; i < 1000; i++) count++;` Is it always 2000?
items.answer: Not always 2000. `count++` is read, add, write; two threads can lose updates, so the result can be anything from 1000 to 2000 and typically varies between runs.

blocks.text: #### Threads

items.question: What does this print, and why? `Thread t = new Thread(() ->` `System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName())); t.run();`
items.answer: It prints `main`: `run()` called directly executes on the calling thread; nothing is started.

items.question: A thread calls `lock.wait()`. Which `Thread.State` is it in? What if it calls `Thread.sleep(500)`? What if it tries to enter a `synchronized` block held by another thread?
items.answer: `WAITING`; `TIMED_WAITING`; `BLOCKED`.

items.question: Why is `catch (InterruptedException e) {}` considered a bug?
items.answer: It swallows the cancellation request. The interrupt flag was cleared when the exception was thrown, so nobody up the stack can learn that the thread was asked to stop. Rethrow, or restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`.

items.question: When does the JVM exit with respect to daemon and non-daemon threads? What happens to a daemon thread's `finally` block at that moment?
items.answer: It exits when the last non-daemon thread ends. Daemon threads are killed abruptly, so their `finally` blocks may not run.

items.question: What happens if you call `start()` twice on the same `Thread` object?
items.answer: `IllegalThreadStateException`. Create a new `Thread` (or submit the task again to a pool).

items.question: A thread throws an uncaught `RuntimeException` inside `run()`. Does `main`'s `try/catch` around `t.start()` catch it?
items.answer: No. The exception happens on the other thread. It goes to that thread's uncaught-exception handler, by default printing the stack trace; `main` is unaffected.

blocks.text: #### Races and the Java Memory Model

items.question: Two threads each execute `counter++` 1000 times on a shared `volatile int counter` starting at 0. Can the final value be less than 2000? Why?
items.answer: Yes. `volatile` makes each read and write visible, but `counter++` is read-modify-write; two threads can read the same value and both store value+1. Use `AtomicInteger` or `synchronized`.

items.question: A worker loops `while (running) { process(); }` and another thread sets `running = false`. Name the bug if `running` is a plain `boolean`, and give the smallest fix.
items.answer: A visibility bug: the worker may never see the write (the JIT can hoist the read). Declare the field `volatile`.

items.question: State the happens-before rule for `Thread.join()`. Why does it let you read a result field written by the joined thread without any other synchronisation?
items.answer: Everything the thread did happens-before the return of `join()` in the waiting thread. So after `join()` returns, all of the thread's writes are visible.

items.question: What is wrong with this code? Fix it. `private static Resource r; static Resource get() { if (r == null) r` `= new Resource(); return r; }`
items.answer: Two threads can both see null and create two instances (a check-then-act race), and a thread may see a partially built object. Fix: make `get() synchronized`, or use the holder idiom, or `volatile` plus double-checked locking.

items.question: Why is a class whose fields are all `final` easier to share between threads? Which condition must still hold in the constructor?
items.answer: The freeze rule makes final fields visible after construction even if the reference was published by a race, and nothing changes afterwards. The constructor must not let `this` escape before it finishes.

items.question: True or false: a `volatile` write happens-before every later read of the same variable, so after thread B reads `ready` `== true` it also sees everything thread A wrote before setting `ready`.
items.answer: True. Program order plus the volatile rule plus transitivity make all earlier writes of A visible to B (the piggybacking effect).

blocks.text: #### synchronized and Monitors

items.question: What object does each lock on? `static synchronized void a()`, `synchronized void b()`, `synchronized (this)` `{ }`.
items.answer: `a()`: the `Class` object. `b()` and the block: `this`. So `b()` and the block exclude each other, but `a()` does not exclude either.

items.question: Why does this fail? `synchronized void push(int x) { list.add(x); } int size() { return list.size(); }` (the list is a shared `ArrayList`)
items.answer: `size()` is not synchronised, so it may read the list without a happens-before edge from `push` (stale or inconsistent size, possible failure during a resize). All accesses to shared state must use the same lock.

items.question: What exception is thrown by `lock.wait()` when the caller does not own the lock's monitor? What does `wait` do with the monitor it owns?
items.answer: `IllegalMonitorStateException`. `wait` releases the monitor while waiting and reacquires it before returning.

items.question: What is wrong with `synchronized (lock) { if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); item = queue.remove(); }` and how do you fix it?
items.answer: `if` instead of `while`: after a spurious or stolen wake-up the queue may still be empty and `remove()` throws `NoSuchElementException`. Use `while (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait();`.

items.question: Thread 1 locks A then B; thread 2 locks B then A. Name the problem and two fixes.
items.answer: Deadlock through opposite lock ordering. Fixes: acquire in a single global order; use one lock for both; use `tryLock` with timeout and back off.

items.question: You get a thread dump of a hung service. Which states and lines indicate a deadlock?
items.answer: Threads in `BLOCKED (on object monitor)` with `waiting to lock <addr>`, where the lock is held by another waiting thread in a cycle; `jstack` prints "Found one Java-level deadlock".

blocks.text: #### Thread Confinement, Immutability and Liveness

items.question: What does this program print, and why does it matter in a thread pool? `static ThreadLocal<String> user = new` `ThreadLocal<>();` Task 1 on pool thread P calls `user.set("alice")` and ends. Task 2 later runs on P and calls `user.get()`.
items.answer: Task 2 prints `alice` (the stale value), because the value is stored on the thread, not the task. This leaks identity between requests; always call `remove()` in `finally`.

items.question: Is a `record Order(String id, List<String> items)` immutable? How would you make it so?
items.answer: Only shallowly: the `items` list may be mutated by whoever holds it. Make a defensive copy in a compact constructor: `items = List.copyOf(items);`.

items.question: List the three levels of thread confinement. Which one is checked by the compiler?
items.answer: Stack confinement (locals), ad hoc confinement (convention), `ThreadLocal`. None of them is enforced by the type system; the nearest is stack confinement by never letting a local object escape.

items.question: What does each of these look like in a thread dump: deadlock, livelock? What differs in CPU usage?
items.answer: Deadlock: BLOCKED/WAITING threads in a cycle, CPU idle, and `jstack` reports the deadlock. Livelock: threads RUNNABLE or alternating, CPU busy, no progress.

items.question: Why can a fixed thread pool of 2 threads deadlock when each task submits a subtask to the same pool and waits for its result?
items.answer: Both pool threads are occupied by the parent tasks, blocked in `Future.get()`; the subtasks wait in the queue for a free thread that never comes. Use a bigger or separate pool, or avoid blocking on subtasks.

items.question: Why is `new ReentrantLock()` not fair by default? What does `new ReentrantLock(true)` change?
items.answer: Fairness costs throughput, since a barging thread can take a just-released lock without the cost of waking a queued thread. `true` makes the lock grant to the longest-waiting thread, reducing starvation but lowering throughput.

blocks.text: #### Locks and Atomics

items.question: Why must `lock.lock()` come before the `try` block, and `unlock()` be in `finally`?
items.answer: If `lock()` is inside the `try` and fails, `finally` would unlock a lock you do not own (`IllegalMonitorStateException`), masking the real error. `finally` guarantees release on every exit path, including exceptions.

items.question: What is wrong with this code? `rw.readLock().lock(); cache.put(k, v); rw.writeLock().lock();` (the thread already holds the read lock).
items.answer: A read lock cannot be upgraded. The blocking `writeLock().lock()` waits for all readers to leave, including this thread, so it deadlocks. Release the read lock first, then take the write lock and recheck.

items.question: Two threads each run `for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) volatile_counter++;`. Can the final value be less than 2000? Why?
items.answer: Yes, it can be less than 2000 (typically is). `volatile` gives visibility but `++` is read-modify-write, so increments are lost when threads interleave.

items.question: When would you choose `LongAdder` over `AtomicLong`, and when not?
items.answer: `LongAdder` for write-heavy counters (metrics) read rarely, where contention makes CAS retry. `AtomicLong` when you need the exact value atomically, such as an ID sequence, or when contention is low.

items.question: In `updateAndGet(x -> x + sideEffect())` why is a side effect in the lambda a bug?
items.answer: The function may be re-executed each time the CAS fails, so the side effect would happen an unpredictable number of times.

items.question: What does the stamp in `AtomicStampedReference` protect against?
items.answer: The ABA problem: the value changing A to B and back to A between your read and your CAS. The stamp changes on every update, so the CAS fails.

blocks.text: #### Executors and Thread Pools

items.question: A pool is created with core 4, max 16 and `new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()`. A flood of tasks arrives. How many threads will the pool ever have, and why?
items.answer: Four. The unbounded queue never reports full, so step 3 (grow toward max) never happens; `maximumPoolSize` is never reached.

items.question: What is wrong here? `pool.submit(() -> { riskyWork(); });` and nobody keeps the returned Future.
items.answer: The exception is captured in the Future and never seen. Either call `get()` / handle failures inside the task, or use `execute()`, or catch and log in the task.

items.question: What does `shutdown()` do to tasks already waiting in the queue? What about `shutdownNow()`?
items.answer: `shutdown()` lets queued tasks run to completion but accepts no new ones. `shutdownNow()` does not run queued tasks, returns them as a list, and interrupts the running ones.

items.question: You run `ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 1, SECONDS)` and `task` throws on its 5th run. What happens to runs 6, 7, ...?
items.answer: They never happen. A throwing periodic task cancels its own future silently. Catch exceptions inside the task.

items.question: Which rejection policy gives back-pressure, and how does it work?
items.answer: `CallerRunsPolicy`: the submitting thread runs the task itself, so it cannot submit more until it finishes, slowing the producer to the pace of the workers.

items.question: A task calls `pool.submit(sub).get()` and the pool has 2 threads. Two such tasks run at once. What happens?
items.answer: Both workers are blocked in `get()` waiting for subtasks that sit in the queue with no free thread: a thread-pool deadlock. Use another pool or non-blocking composition.

blocks.text: #### CompletableFuture

items.question: What is the type of `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 5).thenApply(x ->` `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> x))`, and how would you fix it?
items.answer: `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Integer>>`. Use `thenCompose` instead of `thenApply`.

items.question: What does this print? `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 1 / 0).exceptionally(e -> -1).thenApply(x ->` `x * 10).join()`
items.answer: `-10`. The division fails, `exceptionally` supplies -1, then `thenApply` multiplies it.

items.question: Why is `supplyAsync(() -> jdbc.query(...))` without an executor a bad idea?
items.answer: A blocking call ties up a common-pool thread, starving parallel streams and other async work; with a small CPU count the pool is tiny. Pass a dedicated executor.

items.question: A chain of three `thenApply` calls ends without `join()` and without `exceptionally`. Stage two throws. What do you observe?
items.answer: Nothing: no output and no exception. The failure sits in the final future and is lost unless something reads it or handles it.

items.question: After `future.orTimeout(1, SECONDS)` fails with `TimeoutException`, is the supplier still running?
items.answer: Yes. `orTimeout` only completes the future exceptionally; it does not interrupt or stop the computation.

items.question: `anyOf(a, b)`: a fails immediately, b would succeed in one second. What is the result?
items.answer: The result future completes exceptionally with a's exception, because `anyOf` takes the first completion, successful or not.

blocks.text: #### Synchronizers and Concurrent Collections

items.question: What is wrong with `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);` on a `ConcurrentHashMap`, and what is the fix?
items.answer: Check-then-act race: two threads can both see the key absent and both put. Use `putIfAbsent(k, v)` or `computeIfAbsent(k, fn)`, which are atomic.

items.question: A worker may throw before it reaches `latch.countDown()`. What happens to `latch.await()`, and how do you prevent it?
items.answer: It hangs forever, since the count never reaches zero. Put `countDown()` in a `finally` block.

items.question: What does this print? `var l = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2)); for (int x : l) { l.add(x +` `10); } System.out.println(l);`
items.answer: `[1, 2, 11, 12]`. The loop iterates the snapshot `[1, 2]` (no exception), and each iteration appends `x + 10` to the live list.

items.question: You need at most 4 concurrent calls to a rate-limited API from 50 threads. Which class, and which two calls?
items.answer: `Semaphore(4)`: `acquire()` before the call and `release()` in `finally`.

items.question: Why does `ConcurrentHashMap` reject `null` values?
items.answer: `get(k) == null` would be ambiguous (absent versus mapped to null), and in a concurrent map you cannot resolve it with a second `containsKey` call because the state may change in between.

items.question: Which `BlockingQueue` method does not block and returns `false` when the queue is full? Which one blocks forever?
items.answer: `offer(e)` returns `false` immediately when full; `put(e)` blocks until space is available.

blocks.text: #### Virtual Threads

items.question: Why is `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` not a "pool"? What would you use to cap concurrency?
items.answer: It does not reuse or limit threads: every task gets a fresh virtual thread. Cap concurrency with a `Semaphore` (acquire before the call, release in `finally`).

items.question: What does this print on Java 21? `Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> {});` `System.out.println(t.getState() + " " + t.isDaemon());`
items.answer: `NEW true`. Virtual threads are always daemon threads, and an unstarted one is in state `NEW`.

items.question: A virtual thread does `synchronized (lock) { Thread.sleep(1000); }` on Java 21 with 4 CPUs. What happens to its carrier, and what changed in Java 24?
items.answer: The carrier is pinned and blocked for the full second, unusable by other virtual threads. Java 24 (JEP 491) lets the virtual thread release the carrier even inside `synchronized`.

items.question: Will 10,000 virtual threads each running `while (true) { x++; }` all make progress on a 4-CPU machine? Why or why not?
items.answer: No. Scheduling is cooperative: a CPU-bound virtual thread never blocks, so it never unmounts. Only 4 run at a time, each holding its carrier until it ends (never, here); the other 9,996 starve.

items.question: Why is a thread-per-request design with platform threads limited, and what limit remains with virtual threads?
items.answer: Each platform thread costs OS resources and memory, so a few thousand is the practical ceiling. With virtual threads the remaining limits are the downstream resources (database connections, sockets, rate limits) and CPU for the actual work.

items.question: Why is putting a 500 KB buffer in a `ThreadLocal` a worse idea with virtual threads than with a 200-thread pool?
items.answer: Each virtual thread would get its own 500 KB copy; with 100,000 concurrent virtual threads that is about 50 GB. A pool of 200 threads holds 200 copies, about 100 MB.
